questions.q: Case: Compulsive porn use harming sleep and relationships. Best response?
questions.why: Compulsive use is best handled with counselling (such as CBT), blocking software, addressing underlying stress and help like 14416. More use, hiding it or ignoring it doesn't help.

questions.q: Which combination best protects reproductive health in adults?
options: Vaccines, screening, STI testing, qualified care
questions.why: Reproductive health is protected by vaccines, screening, STI testing and care from qualified doctors. Herbal boosters, online pills and avoiding doctors add risk.

options: Knowing what's normal helps spot changes early
questions.why: Knowing what is normal for your body helps you notice changes early and see a doctor sooner. It does not diagnose cancer or replace doctors.

courses.title: Revision & Practice · Reproductive health
courses.summary: Formula-and-facts revision for human reproduction (NEET/board level), contraception, STIs/HIV, pregnancy law and adult health, plus a 20-question mock.
outcomes: Learners can recall key reproductive biology facts and numbers
Learners can compare contraceptive methods and state key laws
Learners can solve numerical and case-based questions
courses.guardianNote: Revision of reproductive biology, contraception, STIs/HIV and reproductive law at senior-secondary/NEET level; clinical and non-explicit.

scenes.text: Kriti writes every reproduction number on one card.
She revises it on the bus daily.
In the mock test, the numbers questions are her easiest marks.

steps.title: Biology
steps.body: Fertilisation: ampulla. Implantation: endometrium, ~day 6–7. Spermatogenesis: 1 primary spermatocyte → 4 sperm; oogenesis: 1 → 1 ovum + polar bodies. Ovulation: LH surge; ≈ cycle length − 14. Corpus luteum → progesterone; hCG maintains it. Oxytocin (labour, positive feedback, let-down), prolactin (milk). Naegele: LMP − 3 months + 7 days (+1 year).

steps.title: Contraception (typical-use effectiveness)
steps.body: Male condom ~87% · pill ~93% · injectable ~96% · copper IUD >99% · sterilisation >99% · withdrawal ~80%. EC pill ≤72 h (sooner better); copper IUD ≤5 days. Only condoms prevent STIs.

steps.title: STIs & HIV
steps.body: Curable: chlamydia, gonorrhoea, syphilis, trichomoniasis. Viral: HIV, herpes, HPV, hepatitis B. HPV & Hep B vaccines. PEP ≤72 h. U=U. NACO 1097. HIV/AIDS Act 2017 bans discrimination.

steps.title: Law & services
steps.body: Age of consent 18 (POCSO). MTP (Amendment) Act 2021: ≤20 wk one RMP; 20–24 wk two RMPs (specified categories); >24 wk Medical Board for foetal abnormalities. PCPNDT bans sex determination. ART & Surrogacy Acts 2021. VIA screening 30–65.

quiz.why: Ovulation occurs about 14 days before the next period. In a 28-day cycle, 28 − 14 = day 14.

scenes.text: The class does a 10-minute numericals sprint.
Ovulation days, due dates, gamete counts, failure rates.
Practice turns them into one-step questions.

steps.title: Worked set
steps.body:
1. 120 primary spermatocytes → **480 sperm**.
2. 75 primary oocytes → **75 ova**.
3. Cycle 26 days → ovulation day **12**.
4. LMP 15 August → due ≈ **22 May** next year.
5. 2,000 users of a 7%-failure method → **140** pregnancies/year.
6. Unprotected sex Tue 10 pm → EC pill by **Fri 10 pm**; copper IUD by **Sun 10 pm**.

steps.title: Method for every numerical
steps.body:
1. Write the formula first (e.g. ovulation day = cycle length − 14).
2. Substitute numbers with units.
3. Sanity-check: is the answer plausible (a day within the cycle, a date ~9 months later)?

steps.title: Common slips
steps.body: Forgetting polar bodies; counting ovulation from the start instead of subtracting 14 from cycle length; adding 3 months instead of subtracting in Naegele's rule.

activity.prompt: LMP-based: a cycle is 33 days long. On which cycle day does ovulation usually occur (luteal phase 14 days)?

quiz.why: A primary spermatocyte undergoes meiosis to form 4 sperm. So 90 × 4 = 360 sperm.
Ovulation is about 14 days before the next period. For a 31-day cycle, 31 − 14 = day 17.
Naegele's rule: subtract 3 months, then add 7 days. 1 February − 3 months = 1 November, + 7 days = 8 November.

scenes.text: A visiting doctor brings anonymised case cards.
Students identify the issue and the right next step.
Clear thinking: biology + law + compassion.

steps.title: Case 1
steps.body: Condom broke, 30 hours ago → EC pill now (or copper IUD within 5 days); consider STI testing.

steps.title: Case 2
steps.body: Needle-stick injury in a hospital → PEP ASAP within 72 h; report and test.

steps.title: Case 3
steps.body: Couple, 2 years trying → evaluate both; semen analysis + ovulation tests.

steps.title: Case 4
steps.body: Irregular 60-day cycles, acne, hair growth, 18 → PCOS evaluation.

steps.title: Case 5
steps.body: A family wants to know the baby's sex by ultrasound → illegal under PCPNDT; doctors must refuse.

activity.prompt: Match the case to the action

quiz.why: A condom that broke 30 hours ago leaves time for emergency contraception, which works best the sooner it is taken (the pill within 72 hours). Waiting or doing nothing risks pregnancy.
After a needle-stick injury, start PEP as soon as possible and within 72 hours, and get medical advice. Ignoring it or taking antibiotics won't stop HIV.
A request for sex determination is illegal under the PCPNDT Act. It is not a private choice.
Both partners should be evaluated for infertility, since male and female factors both contribute.

questions.why: Fertilisation takes place in the ampulla of the fallopian tube. Implantation, not fertilisation, happens in the uterus.
Only condoms protect against STIs as well as pregnancy, because they act as a barrier. The IUD, injectable and pill prevent pregnancy only.
The NACO national AIDS helpline is 1097. 1098 is Childline, 1930 is cybercrime and 181 is the Women's Helpline.
The age of consent in India is 18, and under POCSO anyone under 18 is a child.
A surge of LH (luteinising hormone) from the pituitary triggers ovulation. Oxytocin and prolactin have other roles.
The copper IUD is over 99% effective because it needs no daily action and copper is toxic to sperm.
Syphilis is bacterial, so antibiotics cure it. HIV, herpes and HPV are viral and not simply cured.
Antara is an injectable contraceptive (DMPA) given every 3 months. It isn't an IUD, pill or condom.

questions.q: Assertion: Maternal and foetal blood don't mix directly. Reason: Exchange occurs across placental membranes.
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. Maternal and foetal blood stay separate, and exchange of nutrients and gases occurs across the placental membranes.
A secondary oocyte is released at ovulation arrested in metaphase II. It finishes meiosis II only if a sperm enters.
Up to 20 weeks, one registered medical practitioner (RMP) is enough to approve MTP. Two RMPs are needed between 20 and 24 weeks for special categories.

options: undetectable viral load preventing sexual transmission
questions.why: U=U means an undetectable viral load on ART prevents sexual transmission of HIV. It is not a cure, vaccine or test.
Each primary spermatocyte gives 4 sperm. So 150 × 4 = 600 sperm.
Ovulation is about 14 days before the next period, so for a 34-day cycle, 34 − 14 = day 20.
Naegele's rule: 25 December − 3 months = 25 September, then + 7 days = 2 October (of the next year).

questions.q: Case: Exposure Thursday 11 pm. Latest PEP start:
questions.why: PEP must start within 72 hours of exposure. Thursday 11 pm + 3 days = Sunday 11 pm.

questions.q: Case: Unmarried woman, contraceptive failure, 12 weeks. MTP?
options: Eligible; one RMP up to 20 weeks
questions.why: After the 2021 amendment, an unmarried woman with contraceptive failure is eligible, and one RMP can approve MTP up to 20 weeks. So at 12 weeks no Medical Board or court is needed.

questions.q: Why does menstruation follow if no fertilisation?
questions.why: If there is no fertilisation, the corpus luteum regresses and progesterone falls, so the endometrium sheds as menstruation. A rise in hCG would instead maintain pregnancy.

options: The EC pill ends an established pregnancy
questions.why: The false statement is that the EC pill ends an established pregnancy. It works mainly by delaying ovulation and is not an abortion pill; the other three statements are true.

well-safety.title: Safe & strong: body safety, online safety & bullying
well-safety.description: Personal safety and body autonomy for every age band, abuse and grooming awareness with POCSO basics, online safety and sextortion response, and bullying, cyberbullying and ragging — calm, practical and help-focused.

courses.title: My body belongs to me (ages 4–8)
courses.summary: A gentle first safety course to share with a grown-up: naming body parts correctly, private parts, safe and unsafe touch, the 'No–Go–Tell' rule, secrets vs surprises, and choosing your trusted grown-ups.
outcomes: Children can name body parts including private parts with correct words
Children can tell safe from unsafe touch
Children can use No–Go–Tell
Children can tell secrets from surprises
Children can name trusted grown-ups
courses.guardianNote: For ages 4–8 with a parent or teacher: correct names for body parts, 'my body belongs to me', safe and unsafe touch, secrets vs surprises and telling a trusted adult. Simple, warm and non-frightening; no images beyond emoji. Recommended in UNESCO ITGSE 2018 for this age.

scenes.text: At bath time, Mummy names body parts with Chintu: elbow, knee, tummy.
'And these are private parts — penis for boys, vulva for girls. Bottoms are private too.'
Chintu giggles, then says them proudly. Naming is normal!

steps.title: Every part has a name
steps.body: Head, shoulders, knees, toes, tummy, back… and **private parts**: the parts covered by underwear or a swimsuit. Boys have a **penis**; girls have a **vulva**; everyone has a **bottom** (and girls' chests become private as they grow). Using real names helps you tell a grown-up clearly if something is wrong.
steps.say: Every part of your body has a name. Private parts are the parts covered by your underwear.

steps.title: The swimsuit rule
steps.body: Private parts are the parts your **swimsuit or underwear covers**. They are just for you.

steps.title: Grown-ups who may help
steps.body: When you're little, a parent or carer may help you wash or use the toilet, and a doctor may check you **with your parent there**. They tell you why. That's OK.

steps.title: Grown-up note
steps.body: Use correct words calmly, without giggles or shame. Children who know correct terms are better able to report abuse.

items.say: Private parts are covered by my underwear. They are just for me.

quiz.q: Private parts are the parts covered by…
quiz.why: Private parts are the parts covered by a swimsuit or underwear. This is the swimsuit rule, and it helps you remember which parts are private.

quiz.q: Is it okay to say 'penis' and 'vulva'?
quiz.why: Yes, penis and vulva are the real names for body parts, just like arm or nose. Using real names helps you tell a grown-up clearly if something is wrong.
A doctor may check your body only with your parent there, and they should tell you why. A check should never be secret or alone.

scenes.text: Dadi hugs Meera and it feels warm and happy.
At a party, an uncle tickles Meera too hard and won't stop when she says no.
Meera tells Mummy. Mummy says, 'You did the right thing. Your body belongs to you.'

steps.title: Safe touch
steps.body: Feels good and kind: a hug from family you like, holding hands to cross the road, a high-five, a doctor's check with your parent there.

steps.title: Unsafe touch
steps.body: Hurts you, scares you, feels yucky or confusing, or is touching your **private parts** (or someone asking you to touch theirs, or to look at private pictures). **It is never your fault.**

steps.title: You can say NO
steps.body: Even to people you know — even to grown-ups — you can say **'NO! Stop!'** You don't have to hug or kiss anyone if you don't want to. You can give a high-five or wave instead.

steps.title: Grown-up note
steps.body: Most harm to children is by someone they know. Don't force children to hug relatives; offer a wave or high-five instead. Respect their 'no'.

items.text: Holding Papa's hand to cross the road
Tickling that doesn't stop when you say no
A hug from Nani that you like

quiz.q: If touch feels yucky or scary, you can say…
quiz.why: If a touch feels yucky or scary, you can say 'NO! Stop!' Your body is yours, and you can say no to touch you don't like.

quiz.q: Do you have to hug everyone?
options: No, you can wave or high-five
quiz.why: No, you don't have to hug anyone. You can choose to wave or give a high-five instead, because your body belongs to you.
Unsafe touch is never your fault. The grown-up or older person is the one who did wrong.

scenes.text: At the park a man says to Arjun, 'Come see my puppy in my car.'
Arjun remembers: NO, GO, TELL!
He runs to his mum and tells her. Mum hugs him: 'Well done!'

steps.title: Three steps
steps.body:
1. **NO** — say it loudly.
2. **GO** — get away to a safe place or grown-up.
3. **TELL** — tell a trusted grown-up straight away. If they don't listen, **tell another**, and keep telling.

steps.title: Tricky situations
steps.body: Someone asks you to keep a touch secret · offers sweets, toys or a phone game to come with them · asks to take photos of you without clothes · says your parent sent them but you don't know the password. → **No – Go – Tell.**

steps.title: Family password
steps.body: Agree a secret family password. If someone says 'Your mother sent me', ask for the password. No password → don't go.

steps.title: Help number
steps.body: Grown-ups can call **1098** (Childline) any time if a child needs help.

activity.prompt: Put the safety steps in order

quiz.why: The three steps are No, Go, Tell. Say no, go away to a safe place, and tell a trusted grown-up.
If one grown-up doesn't listen, keep telling until someone does. Tell another grown-up you trust.

quiz.q: Someone without the family password says Mum sent them…
quiz.why: If someone doesn't know the family password, don't go with them, even if they say Mum sent them. The password keeps you safe.

lessons.title: Secrets vs surprises & my trusted grown-ups

scenes.text: Tara and Mummy are planning a surprise cake for Papa.
'It's a surprise — we'll tell him on Sunday!'
'Surprises are happy and we tell them soon. Secrets that feel bad, we tell right away.'

steps.title: Surprise
steps.body: A happy thing that everyone will find out about soon — like a birthday gift. **OK to keep for a little while.**

steps.title: Unsafe secret
steps.body: Makes you feel worried, scared or confused, or someone says 'never tell or you'll be in trouble'. **Always tell a trusted grown-up**, even if you promised.

steps.title: My helping hand
steps.body: Trace your hand. On each finger write or draw **one trusted grown-up** you could tell — e.g. Mummy, Papa, Nani, class teacher, school nurse.

steps.title: Grown-up note
steps.body: Say often: 'You can tell me anything. You won't be in trouble for telling.' Stay calm if a child tells you something worrying; thank them, believe them, and get help (1098).

items.text: 'If you tell, I'll hurt your puppy'
Someone showed you rude pictures and said keep quiet

quiz.why: A surprise is a happy thing, like a birthday gift, and it is told soon. It is not a secret to keep forever.

quiz.q: A secret that feels bad, you should…
quiz.why: A secret that feels bad should be told to a trusted grown-up. Bad secrets can hurt you, so don't keep them.

quiz.q: How many trusted grown-ups on your helping hand?
quiz.why: You can have five trusted grown-ups, one for each finger on your helping hand. More helpers mean more people to tell.

questions.why: Private parts are covered by underwear or a swimsuit. That is an easy way to remember them.
Safe touch feels kind and happy, like a cuddle you like. Touch that feels yucky or scary is not safe.
The steps are No, Go, Tell: say no, go to a safe place, and tell a trusted grown-up.
Unsafe touch is never your fault. The person who did it is the one who did wrong.

questions.q: You may say no to a hug from…
questions.why: You can say no to a hug from anyone, even family. Your body belongs to you, and you can wave or high-five instead.

questions.q: A birthday gift plan is a…
questions.why: A birthday gift plan is a happy surprise that will be told soon. It is not a bad secret or a lie.

questions.q: 'Don't tell or you'll be in trouble' is…
questions.why: 'Don't tell or you'll be in trouble' is an unsafe secret, so tell a trusted grown-up. Safe surprises don't make you scared.

questions.q: If the first grown-up doesn't listen…
questions.why: If the first grown-up doesn't listen, tell another one. Keep telling until someone helps.
Childline's number is 1098, and you can call it for help. It is free.

questions.q: Someone says 'Mum sent me' but doesn't know the family password. You…
options: don't go and tell a grown-up
questions.why: If they don't know the family password, don't go with them and tell a grown-up. The password helps you know who is safe.

questions.q: Why use real names for private parts?
options: So you can tell a grown-up clearly
questions.why: We use real names for private parts so we can tell a grown-up clearly if something is wrong. The names are not rude or a joke.

questions.q: A doctor checking you is OK when…
options: your parent is there and they tell you why
questions.why: A doctor check is OK when your parent is there and the doctor tells you why. It should never be secret.

questions.q: Someone asks to take photos of you without clothes. You…
questions.why: If someone asks for photos of you without clothes, say No, go, tell. That is unsafe and a grown-up must know.

questions.q: Uncle keeps tickling after you said stop. That is…
questions.why: If your uncle keeps tickling after you said stop, that is not OK, so tell a grown-up. It is not your fault.

questions.q: Who can be a trusted grown-up?
questions.why: Trusted grown-ups include parents, teachers and the school nurse. A stranger online is not a safe person to trust.

courses.title: Safe & strong: consent, privacy and tricky people (ages 6–10)
courses.summary: Asking before touching and accepting 'no', privacy at home and school, early-warning feelings, tricky people (who can be known or unknown), staying safe if lost, and first rules for being online.
outcomes: Children can ask for and give permission and accept 'no'
Children can explain privacy and personal space
Children can notice early-warning feelings
Children can spot tricky-people behaviours and respond
Children can follow a lost-child plan and basic online rules
courses.guardianNote: For children 6–10: asking and giving permission (consent basics), privacy, feelings in the body as safety signals, tricky people (most are not strangers), getting lost, and basic online rules. Calm, non-frightening, and focused on trusted adults and 1098.

scenes.text: Kabir grabs Ayaan's new pencil box without asking. Ayaan feels upset.
Teacher: 'What could Kabir have done?' Class: 'Asked first!'
Next time Kabir asks, 'Can I see it?' Ayaan says, 'Yes, but be careful.'

steps.title: Consent means asking and listening
steps.body: **Consent** = giving permission. Before you touch someone, take their things, or share a photo of them — **ask first**. If they say **no** or look unsure, that means **no**. And you can say no too.

steps.title: Practice lines
steps.body:
- 'Can I give you a hug?' → 'Yes!' (hug) / 'No thanks' (wave instead).
- 'Can I play with your ball?' → 'Not now.' → 'OK!'
- 'Can I post this photo of you?' → 'No.' → don't post it.

steps.title: Personal space bubble
steps.body: Imagine an invisible bubble around each person about an arm's length. Some people like hugs, others don't. **Bodies are different, choices are different, and both are OK.**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking silence means yes — it doesn't.
- Tickling or play-fighting after someone says stop.
- Getting angry when someone says no — it's their right.

statements.s: If someone says no to a hug, you can give a high-five or wave instead.
Silence means yes.
statements.why: Only a clear yes is yes.

statements.s: It's OK to keep tickling a friend who says stop because it's a game.
You should ask before posting a photo of a friend.

quiz.why: Consent means giving permission. You ask first, and the other person decides yes or no.
If a friend looks unsure, treat it as a no and stop. Only a clear, happy yes means yes.

quiz.q: Your personal space bubble is about…
quiz.why: Your personal space bubble is about an arm's length around you. People should ask before coming inside it.
Ask your friend before posting their photo, because it is their picture and their choice.

quiz.q: When someone says no, you should…
quiz.why: When someone says no, accept it. Getting angry, pushing or begging doesn't respect their choice.

scenes.text: A neighbour asks Ria to come inside alone to see kittens. Her tummy feels funny and her heart beats fast.
She remembers: those feelings are early-warning signs.
She says, 'I'll ask my mum first,' and goes home to tell her mum.

steps.title: Early-warning signs
steps.body: Your body warns you when something isn't right: butterflies in the tummy, fast heartbeat, sweaty hands, wanting to cry or run, feeling frozen. **Listen to these feelings** and get to a trusted adult.

steps.title: Privacy
steps.body: Everyone has a right to privacy: using the toilet, bathing and changing alone (once you can), knocking before entering. No one should ask to see your private parts, take photos of them, or show you theirs — except a parent or doctor for health reasons, with you knowing why.

steps.title: Solved example: safe or check?
steps.body:
(a) Doctor checks a rash with Mum present → **safe**.
(b) An older cousin wants to play a 'secret game' with clothes off → **not OK — No, Go, Tell**.
(c) A coach asks you to come to his house alone and not tell parents → **not OK — tell**.

steps.title: Remember
steps.body: Even if you didn't say no, or you said yes at first, or you got a present — if something unsafe happened, **it is never your fault**. Tell a trusted adult or call **1098**.

activity.prompt: Match the feeling to what it might mean

quiz.why: Early-warning signs, like a tight tummy or racing heart, are your body's alarm. They tell you something may be unsafe, so listen to them.

quiz.q: A 'secret game' with clothes off is…
quiz.why: A 'secret game' with clothes off is not OK. Use No, Go, Tell and tell a trusted grown-up.

quiz.q: If something unsafe happened after you got a present…
quiz.why: If something unsafe happened after you got a present, it is still not your fault. Gifts never make unsafe touch OK.
Knocking before entering shows respect for someone's privacy. Everyone has the right to private space.
1098 is the Childline number, a free helpline for children who need help.

scenes.text: At a crowded Diwali mela, Zoya loses her parents' hands.
She stays where she is, then goes to a lady with children at a stall and says, 'I'm lost. My mum's number is…'
Her parents find her in ten minutes. They had practised this at home.

steps.title: Tricky people (not just strangers)
steps.body: Most people are kind. A **tricky person** — known or unknown — might ask a child for help (grown-ups should ask grown-ups), offer gifts or treats to go somewhere, say 'keep it secret', try to get you alone, or ask you to break family rules. **It's the behaviour that matters, not whether you know them.**

steps.title: If you get lost
steps.body:
1. **Stop** and stay near where you lost your grown-up.
2. Look for a **safe helper**: a police officer, a shop counter worker, a mother with children, a security guard in uniform.
3. Say your name and your parent's phone number (learn it by heart!).
4. Never leave with anyone who says they'll take you to your parents.

steps.title: Solved example: what would you do?
steps.body:
(a) A car stops: 'Help me find my lost dog!' → Step back, say 'No', go to your grown-up. Adults ask adults for help.
(b) A family friend says 'Come to my house, don't tell Mum' → **No, Go, Tell**.
(c) A man at the bus stop offers chocolate → 'No thanks', stay with your group.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking only scary-looking strangers are dangerous.
- Wandering off to search for parents.
- Not knowing a parent's phone number.

a.text: You're lost in a big shopping mall.

choices.label: Stay nearby and look for a shop counter worker or security in uniform
Run outside to the parking area to look
choices.feedback: Going far makes it harder to find you.

x.text: It's busy and confusing outside. What now?

choices.label: Go back inside and ask a shop worker for help

b.text: The worker asks your parent's phone number.

choices.label: Say it clearly — you learnt it by heart
You don't know it

b2.text: The worker makes an announcement instead.

choices.label: Wait with the worker

quiz.why: Tricky people are known by what they do, such as asking you to keep secrets, not by how they look. Looks, clothes or cars can't tell you.
When lost, stop and stay nearby, then find a safe helper. Running far or going with anyone makes it harder to be found.

options: a shop counter worker or uniformed guard
quiz.why: A safe helper is someone like a shop counter worker or a uniformed guard, who has a job to help. Random teenagers or people in cars are not safe choices.

quiz.q: Grown-ups who need help should ask…
quiz.why: Grown-ups who need help should ask other grown-ups, not children. An adult asking a child for help is a red flag.
Learn your parent's phone number by heart, so a safe helper can call them if you're lost.

scenes.text: In an online game, a player asks 8-year-old Aarav his school name and for a selfie.
Aarav remembers his rules: no personal info, no photos, tell a grown-up.
He shows Papa, who helps him block and report the player.

steps.title: Golden rules
steps.body:
- Keep private: full name, school, address, phone, passwords, photos.
- Only chat with people you know in real life, with a grown-up's OK.
- Never meet an online 'friend' in person.
- If something online makes you feel scared, sad or confused — **stop, close it, tell a grown-up**.
- It's never your fault if you see something upsetting.

steps.title: Passwords
steps.body: Strong passwords are long (e.g. three random words), different for each account, and shared only with your parent — not friends.

steps.title: Solved example: safe or unsafe?
steps.body:
(a) A 'kid' online asks you to keep your chat secret → **unsafe — tell**.
(b) Your teacher's class video call → **safe**.
(c) A pop-up says 'You won a free phone, enter your address' → **scam — close it**.
(d) A friend sends a funny cartoon → **fine**; ask before forwarding others' photos.

steps.title: Grown-up note
steps.body: Keep devices in shared spaces for young children, use parental controls and age ratings, and talk regularly about what they do online.

activity.prompt: OK to share online, or keep private?

options: close it and tell a grown-up
quiz.why: If something online scares you, close it and tell a grown-up. Don't keep it secret or keep watching.
Never meet an online 'friend' in person, because you can't be sure who they really are. Meeting family or teachers is fine.

quiz.q: A pop-up says you won a phone:
quiz.why: A pop-up saying you won a phone is probably a scam. Close it and don't share your address or pay.
Share passwords only with your parent. Friends and online players could misuse them.
A strong password is long and unique. Short or common ones like 1234 or 'password' are easy to guess.

questions.why: Consent means permission. You must ask first and accept the answer.
Childline's number is 1098, a free helpline for children.

options: stay nearby and find a safe helper
questions.why: If lost, stay nearby and find a safe helper, such as a shop counter worker. Don't leave with anyone or run far.
Silence is not a yes. Wait for a clear yes before going ahead.
Early-warning feelings tell you something may be wrong. Listen to them and tell a grown-up.
Online, keep your address and school private. A stranger could use them to find you.

options: ask you to keep secrets from parents
questions.why: A tricky person might ask you to keep secrets from your parents. Helpful people don't need secrets.

questions.q: An adult asks a child to help find a dog. This is…
options: a red flag — adults ask adults
questions.why: Adults ask other adults for help, not children, so a grown-up asking a child to help find a dog is a red flag. Tell a trusted grown-up.

questions.q: A safe helper in a mall:
questions.why: A shop counter worker is a safe helper in a mall. Someone in the parking lot, a random car or an online friend are not.

questions.q: A family friend says 'Come home with me, don't tell Mum.' You…
questions.why: Say no and tell Mum. 'Don't tell Mum' makes it an unsafe secret.

questions.q: A friend keeps play-fighting after you say stop. That is…
questions.why: A friend who keeps play-fighting after you said stop is not respecting consent. Say it again and tell a grown-up.

questions.q: An online player asks for a selfie and your school name. You…
questions.why: Refuse, block and tell a grown-up. Never send a selfie or school name to an online player.

questions.q: If something unsafe happened and you said yes at first, it is…
questions.why: Even if you said yes at first, it is still not your fault. You can change your mind at any time, and the other person must respect it.

questions.q: Why learn a parent's phone number by heart?
options: So helpers can call them if you're lost
questions.why: Knowing your parent's number by heart means a safe helper can call them if you're lost, even without a phone.

options: Ask before hugging and accept no
questions.why: The safest choice is to ask before hugging and accept no. Hugging anyone, tickling after stop and posting photos without asking all ignore consent.

courses.summary: Understanding body autonomy and the right to say no, the forms of abuse, how grooming works step by step, what India's POCSO Act says about protecting under-18s, how to tell someone and report, and how to support a friend who discloses.

Calm and empowering, emphasising that it is never the child's fault, with 1098, 112 and the NCPCR POCSO e-box.

story.title: The selfie at the family wedding

scenes.text: At a wedding, an older relative keeps pulling 13-year-old Ishita into tight hugs for selfies.
She feels uncomfortable but worries about being 'rude'.
Her mother notices and says, 'She'd prefer a side-hug or a namaste.' Ishita learns her comfort matters more than politeness.

steps.title: What body autonomy means
steps.body: **Body autonomy** is the right to decide what happens to your own body — who touches you, how, and when. It applies to everyone, at every age, including with family, friends, partners, coaches and teachers. Medical care for children involves parents and doctors, but you can still ask questions and have things explained.

steps.title: Types of boundaries
steps.body:
- **Physical**: touch, personal space.
- **Emotional**: what you share; not being shouted at or humiliated.
- **Digital**: your photos, passwords, location, messages.
- **Material**: your belongings and money.
Healthy people **respect** boundaries without punishing you for setting them.

steps.title: Solved example: set a boundary
steps.body:
Formula: **Name it + state it + offer an alternative (optional).**
'I'm not comfortable with tight hugs. A side-hug or namaste works for me.'
'Please don't post my photo without asking.'
If it's ignored → step away and tell a trusted adult.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking politeness means you must accept unwanted touch.
- 'It's family, so it's fine' — family members must respect boundaries too.
- Feeling guilty for saying no.

activity.text: I'm not comfortable with ___. Instead, ___ works for me.
answers: a side-hug|a namaste|a high-five|a wave|a handshake|asking first

quiz.why: Body autonomy applies to everyone at every age. Your body is yours, even with family members.

options: not posting my photo without asking
quiz.why: A digital boundary is a limit about your online things, like not posting my photo without asking. It protects your privacy.

quiz.q: Healthy people respond to boundaries by…
quiz.why: Healthy people respect your boundaries. Laughing at them, ignoring them or punishing you for them is a warning sign.

options: step away and tell an adult
quiz.why: If a boundary is ignored, step away and tell a trusted adult. It is not your fault and you shouldn't keep quiet.

quiz.q: Politeness means you must accept unwanted touch?
quiz.why: No. Being polite doesn't mean you must accept unwanted touch, even from relatives or at weddings. You can say no kindly.

lessons.title: Forms of abuse — and that it's never your fault

scenes.text: Rohan often comes to school with bruises and says he 'fell'.
He seems scared to go home and rarely has lunch.
His class teacher gently asks if he's safe, listens, and contacts Childline 1098 for advice.

steps.title: Forms of abuse
steps.body:
- **Physical**: hitting, burning, shaking, any deliberate injury (corporal punishment in schools is prohibited in India under the RTE Act).
- **Emotional**: constant threats, humiliation, rejection, terrorising.
- **Sexual**: any sexual contact or activity with a child, showing sexual material to a child, taking sexual photos, or sexual talk — **with or without touching**.
- **Neglect**: not providing food, care, safety, medical help.
- **Online**: grooming, sexual messages, sextortion, cyberbullying.
Abuse can happen in any family, school, community or online, by people of any gender — most often by someone the child **knows and trusts**.

steps.title: Never the child's fault
steps.body: Children are never to blame — not if they didn't fight back, froze, kept quiet, accepted gifts, or felt confused. Freezing is a **normal** body response to fear. Abusers often use shame and threats to keep children silent.

steps.title: Solved example: name it
steps.body:
(a) A tutor shows a student sexual videos → **sexual abuse** (no touching needed).
(b) A parent calls a child worthless every day → **emotional abuse**.
(c) A child is left without food for days → **neglect**.
(d) An adult online asks a 13-year-old for private photos → **online sexual abuse / grooming** — a crime.

steps.title: Where to turn
steps.body: Trusted adult · school counsellor/principal · **Childline 1098** (24×7, free) · **112** if in danger · police. You can tell someone even years later.

activity.prompt: Which form of abuse is described?

items.text: An adult showing a child sexual pictures
No food or medical care for a sick child
Asking a child for private photos

quiz.why: Sexual abuse can happen with or without touching, for example by showing a child sexual material or taking photos. It is not limited to touch.
Freezing is a normal fear response, not consent or the child's fault. The body can freeze when frightened.
Abusers are most often someone the child knows, such as a relative or trusted adult. That is why 'stranger danger' alone is not enough.

quiz.q: Corporal punishment in Indian schools is…
quiz.why: Corporal punishment in schools is prohibited in India under the RTE Act. Schools may not hit or humiliate students.
Childline's helpline number is 1098, for children in trouble. 100 is police and 14416 is the mental health helpline.

lessons.title: Grooming: how it works and how to spot it

scenes.text: A coach gives 12-year-old Neel extra attention, gifts and rides home.
Later he asks Neel to keep their chats secret and messages him late at night.
Neel's sister learns the grooming pattern at school, notices the signs and tells their parents. They report it.

steps.title: The grooming pattern
steps.body:
**Grooming** is when someone builds trust and emotional connection with a child (and often their family) to abuse or exploit them. Common steps:
1. **Targeting** a child who seems lonely or needs attention.
2. **Gaining trust** — of the child and family; being 'helpful'.
3. **Filling a need** — gifts, attention, rides, praise, money, phone recharges.
4. **Isolating** — getting the child alone, private chats.
5. **Testing boundaries & sexualising** — jokes, 'accidental' touch, sexual talk or images.
6. **Secrecy & control** — 'our secret', threats, blame.

steps.title: Red flags in adults
steps.body: Special favours for one child · insisting on time alone · secret messages or gifts · telling the child not to tell parents · ignoring a child's 'no' · sexual jokes or content · moving to private apps.

steps.title: Solved example: count the red flags
steps.body: Coach: gifts ✔, rides alone ✔, secret chats ✔, late-night messages ✔ → **4 red flags** → tell a trusted adult now. Adults who care about children **want** parents involved.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'He's so nice, he can't be harmful' — groomers often appear kind.
- Waiting for proof — patterns are reason enough to tell an adult.
- Feeling disloyal — telling is protecting.

items: Gaining trust of child and family
Filling a need with gifts or attention

options: building trust to abuse or exploit
quiz.why: Grooming is slowly building trust with a child to abuse or exploit them. It isn't normal friendship, tutoring or coaching.

options: 'Don't tell your parents about our chats'
a parent picking up a child
quiz.why: 'Don't tell your parents about our chats' is a red flag, since secrecy is how groomers keep control. Teaching in class or parents picking up a child are normal.
Groomers often seem kind and helpful, which is how they win trust. They rarely seem obvious or scary.
Safe adults want parents involved and aware. Someone who keeps parents out or unaware is a warning sign.

quiz.q: Do you need proof to tell?
quiz.why: No, you don't need proof to tell. Patterns and bad feelings are enough, and telling early helps.

lessons.title: POCSO: your legal protection, and how to tell

scenes.text: Fifteen-year-old Sana is harassed by a neighbour who sends sexual messages.
With her mother she saves screenshots and they file a complaint at the police station; a woman officer records her statement.
Her identity is kept confidential, as the law requires.

steps.title: POCSO Act, 2012 — key points
steps.body:
- Protects **every child under 18** — of any gender — from sexual assault, sexual harassment and use in pornography.
- **Age of consent in India is 18**: any sexual act with a person under 18 is an offence under POCSO.
- **Child-friendly procedures**: statement recorded at a place of the child's choice, preferably by a woman police officer, not in uniform; a support person may be present; the child's **identity must not be disclosed** (including by media).
- **Special courts**; trials meant to be speedy.
- **Mandatory reporting**: anyone who knows of such an offence must report it to the police or Special Juvenile Police Unit.
- Alongside POCSO, the **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS)** and IT Act also apply to sexual offences.

steps.title: How to tell
steps.body:
- Choose someone safe: parent, relative, teacher, counsellor, doctor.
- Say it simply: 'Someone did something that made me uncomfortable. I need help.'
- If they don't believe you, **tell someone else**.
- Report: **Childline 1098**, **112**, local police, or the **NCPCR POCSO e-box** online. Online crimes: **cybercrime.gov.in** or **1930**.
- Save evidence (messages, screenshots) — don't delete, don't forward.

steps.title: Solved example: support a friend who discloses
steps.body:
1. **Listen**, stay calm.
2. **Believe**: 'I believe you.'
3. **Reassure**: 'It's not your fault. Telling was brave.'
4. **Don't promise secrecy**; explain you need to get a trusted adult's help.
5. **Get help** together (1098).
6. Don't confront the abuser yourself.

steps.title: General education
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice. For a specific case, contact Childline 1098, the police, or a lawyer/legal-aid service (DLSA).

activity.prompt: Questions teens rarely ask about abuse

items.q: What if it was someone in my family?
items.a: It's still abuse and still not your fault. You can tell another adult, a teacher or call 1098.

items.q: Will I get in trouble for not telling earlier?
items.a: No. You can tell any time. Many people take time.

items.q: What if I'm a boy — does POCSO protect me?
items.a: Yes. POCSO protects children of every gender.

items.q: Will everyone find out?
items.a: The law requires the child's identity to be kept confidential.

items.q: What if my friend made me promise not to tell?
items.a: Their safety matters more. Tell a trusted adult and support your friend.

options: all children under 18 of any gender
quiz.why: POCSO protects all children under 18 of any gender. It is not just for girls or under-12s.
The age of consent in India is 18, under POCSO. Under 18, a child cannot legally consent to sexual acts.
Under POCSO, the child's identity must not be disclosed, to protect them from harm and stigma. Publishing it is an offence.

quiz.q: Online sexual crimes can be reported at…
quiz.why: Online sexual crimes can be reported at cybercrime.gov.in or the helpline 1930. A friend's group or game chat is not a place to report.
When a friend discloses abuse, listen, believe them and help them get an adult's help. Don't promise secrecy, post online or confront the abuser alone.

options: deciding what happens to your body
questions.why: Body autonomy means you decide what happens to your body. It doesn't mean obeying all adults or always being polite.
Childline's number is 1098, for children in need of help. 100 is police and 14416 is the mental health helpline.
The age of consent in India is 18, under POCSO.

questions.q: Abuse is the child's fault if they froze?
questions.why: No. Abuse is never the child's fault, even if the child froze. Freezing is a normal fear reaction.
Secret gifts and chats are a grooming red flag, since they build secrecy and trust. Parents present, public praise and group coaching are open.
1930 is the national cybercrime helpline. 108 is the ambulance, and 1098 is Childline.

questions.q: Assertion: Sexual abuse can occur without touch. Reason: Showing a child sexual material is abuse.
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. Showing a child sexual material is abuse even without touch.
Under POCSO, reporting is mandatory for anyone who knows about child sexual abuse. It isn't optional or only for parents or doctors.
Daily humiliation and threats are emotional abuse. Bedtime rules, homework correction and coaching feedback are normal.

questions.q: Case: A coach insists on rides alone and secret chats with one student. Best action?
questions.why: A coach who insists on rides alone and secret chats with one student shows grooming red flags. Tell a trusted adult now; waiting for proof can allow harm.

questions.q: Which is the correct grooming order?
options: Target → trust → fill need → isolate → test → secrecy
questions.why: Grooming often follows a pattern: choose a target, build trust, fill a need, isolate the child, test boundaries, then enforce secrecy. The other orders don't match.

options: statement recorded preferably by a woman officer not in uniform
questions.why: POCSO's child-friendly procedure includes recording the child's statement preferably by a woman officer who is not in uniform. Media naming and public hearings are not allowed.

questions.q: A friend discloses abuse and asks you to keep it secret. Best?
options: Reassure, don't promise secrecy, get adult help together
questions.why: Reassure your friend, don't promise secrecy, and get adult help together. Keeping it secret, posting online or confronting the abuser can make things worse.

questions.q: Which law is NOT relevant to child sexual abuse in India?
questions.why: The Motor Vehicles Act deals with traffic and vehicles, not child sexual abuse. BNS, POCSO and the IT Act are all relevant.

questions.q: Case: A 16-year-old says, 'It was my uncle and I didn't stop him, so it's my fault.' Best response?
options: 'It's not your fault; let's get help (1098).'
questions.why: Tell them it is not their fault and get help, such as Childline 1098. Blaming them, telling them to forget it or keeping quiet adds to the harm.

options: To avoid being caught and keep control
questions.why: Abusers demand secrecy to avoid being caught and to keep control over the child. It is never to protect the child.

questions.q: Which evidence advice is right for online harassment?
options: Save screenshots; don't delete or forward; report
questions.why: For online harassment, save screenshots, don't delete or forward them, and report. Deleting loses evidence, and forwarding spreads harm.

courses.title: Online safety, image-sharing & sextortion awareness
courses.summary: Protect your accounts and privacy, spot scams and online grooming, understand the risks and laws around sharing intimate images, know exactly what to do if someone tries sextortion, handle deepfakes, and report safely in India.
outcomes: Learners can secure accounts with strong passwords, 2FA and privacy settings
Learners can spot scams, fake profiles and grooming online
Learners can explain the law and risks around sharing intimate images, especially of under-18s
Learners can follow the sextortion response steps
Learners can report cybercrime and get images taken down
courses.guardianNote: For ages 12–18: online privacy, scams, grooming, image-sharing risks and Indian law, sextortion (what it is and exactly what to do), deepfakes and reporting. Non-explicit and shame-free, focused on protection and getting help (1930, cybercrime.gov.in, 1098, 112).

lessons.title: Lock it down: accounts, privacy and digital footprint

scenes.text: Kriti's Instagram is hacked; the hacker posts scam links to her friends.
She used the same password everywhere and no two-factor authentication.
After recovering it she sets a passphrase, turns on 2FA, and reviews who can see her posts.

steps.title: Account security
steps.body:
- **Long passphrases** (e.g. 3–4 random words) — different for every account; a password manager helps.
- **Two-factor authentication (2FA)** on email and social media.
- **Never share OTPs** — no bank, company or friend legitimately needs them.
- Log out on shared devices; update apps.

steps.title: Privacy settings
steps.body: Private account; approve followers you know; turn off location tagging and live location sharing; limit who can message, tag or mention you; check your profile in 'view as public' mode.

steps.title: Digital footprint
steps.body: What you post can be screenshotted, saved and shared — **'deleted' doesn't mean gone**. Colleges and employers may look at public profiles. Before posting ask: *Would I be OK if my grandparent, principal, or a future employer saw this?*

steps.title: Solved example: password strength
steps.body:
A 6-character password of lowercase letters: 26⁶ ≈ **309 million** combinations — guessable quickly by computers.
A 4-random-word passphrase from a 7,000-word list: 7000⁴ ≈ **2.4 × 10¹⁵** combinations — vastly stronger and easier to remember.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Same password everywhere.
- Posting school uniform + location + daily routine.
- Clicking 'login' links in messages — go to the app directly.

items: Unique passphrase on email and main social app
Never share OTPs — told my family too

options: a second step to log in
quiz.why: 2FA (two-factor authentication) adds a second step to log in, like a code, on top of your password. It stops logins that only know the password.
Never share OTPs with anyone, including callers who say they are from a bank or a delivery agent. An OTP gives access to your account.
Deleted posts are not necessarily gone, since others may have screenshots or copies. So think before posting.
Four random words make a long, hard-to-guess passphrase. Names, 'qwerty' and 123456 are easy to crack.
Avoid login links in messages, as they may be phishing; open the app or site directly. Never reply with your password or forward them.

lessons.title: Scams, fake profiles and online grooming

scenes.text: A profile claiming to be a modelling scout DMs 15-year-old Aisha: 'You could be famous! Send a few photos.'
The account is new, has few real followers and asks her to move to a private app.
Aisha checks with her older cousin, blocks and reports the account.

steps.title: Common scams
steps.body: Fake prizes/lotteries · 'work from home' and part-time job scams · fake customer-care numbers · loan apps · investment/crypto 'doubling' · fake 'digital arrest' calls by people pretending to be police/officials (real police do not arrest or demand money over video calls) · romance and friendship scams · game-currency scams.

steps.title: Grooming online — red flags
steps.body: Lots of flattery quickly · claims to be your age but language feels older · asks for secrecy · wants to move to private or disappearing-message apps · asks for photos, video calls or your location · sends gifts/recharge · turns sexual or asks 'are you alone?' · guilt or threats if you pull back.

steps.title: Solved example: verify a profile
steps.body:
1. Account age and post history? (new, few posts = suspicious)
2. Reverse-image search the profile picture.
3. Mutual friends real?
4. Requests: money, photos, secrecy, moving apps? → **stop**.
5. Tell a trusted adult; block & report.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Trusting a profile because it has a blue tick or many followers (can be bought or faked).
- Paying a 'registration fee' for a job or modelling.
- Staying silent out of embarrassment — scammers count on that.

items.text: Classmate asks about homework in the class group
Pay ₹500 registration for a modelling job
Your aunt shares family photos in the family group

quiz.q: A 'digital arrest' video call demanding money is…
quiz.why: A 'digital arrest' video call demanding money is a scam. Real police and courts don't arrest people over video calls or demand payment.
Asking for secrecy and photos is an online grooming red flag. Memes, group chats and homework talk are normal.

options: check if a photo is stolen
quiz.why: Reverse-image search helps check whether a photo was stolen from elsewhere, for example for fake profiles. It doesn't edit photos or hack accounts.

quiz.q: A job asking for a 'registration fee' is…
quiz.why: A job that asks for a 'registration fee' is likely a scam, since genuine employers don't charge you to hire you.
Blue ticks can be bought or faked, so they are not proof of honesty. Check other signs before trusting.

lessons.title: Image-sharing: risks, consent and the law

scenes.text: Rahul's girlfriend sent him a private photo. After a fight, he forwarded it to a friend.
Within hours it spread across school groups.
The school and police got involved. Rahul learnt that sharing it was a serious offence and caused deep harm.

steps.title: What the law says (India)
steps.body:
- Creating, storing, sharing or asking for **sexual images of anyone under 18** is an offence under the **POCSO Act** and **Section 67B of the IT Act** — even if the person is your age, even if they 'agreed', even if it's a selfie.
- Capturing or sharing someone's **private images without consent** is an offence (**IT Act Section 66E**; publishing sexually explicit material — Sections 67/67A).
- Threatening to share images to get something is **extortion/criminal intimidation** under the **BNS**.

steps.title: Why it's risky
steps.body: Once sent, you lose control: screenshots, forwarding, hacks, break-ups and blackmail. The harm — shame, anxiety, bullying — is real. **Responsibility lies with the person who shares or threatens, not the person in the image.**

steps.title: Solved example: what to do if…
steps.body:
(a) **Someone asks you for a nude**: 'No.' You don't need a reason. Block if they pressure. Tell an adult if they're older or persistent.
(b) **You receive one of someone under 18**: don't forward or save; tell a trusted adult; report and delete as advised.
(c) **You already sent one**: you're not alone and it's not too late — tell a trusted adult; under-18s can use **Take It Down** (by NCMEC) to help stop it spreading on major platforms; report at **cybercrime.gov.in / 1930**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'It's fine because it's my own photo' — for under-18s, it's still illegal and risky.
- Forwarding 'as a joke' — makes you part of the harm and the offence.
- Blaming the person in the photo.

statements.s: Sharing a sexual image of someone under 18 is illegal even if they agreed.
If a photo leaks, the person in it is to blame.
Forwarding a private image 'as a joke' is harmless.
You can say no to sending photos without giving a reason.

options: offence under POCSO and IT Act 67B
quiz.why: Sexual images of under-18s are an offence under POCSO and Section 67B of the IT Act, even if consensual or a selfie. It is never legal.
Sharing private images without consent is an offence under Indian law, such as IT Act 66E. It is not just rude or fine.

options: the person who shares or threatens
quiz.why: Responsibility lies with the person who shares or threatens, not the person in the photo. Victims should not be blamed.

quiz.q: Received a nude of a classmate:
options: don't forward; tell an adult; report
quiz.why: If you receive a nude of a classmate, don't forward it, tell an adult and report it. Forwarding, saving or posting spreads harm and may be an offence.

options: under-18s stop images spreading on platforms
quiz.why: Take It Down is a tool that helps under-18s stop nude images from spreading on platforms. It doesn't delete WhatsApp or edit images.

lessons.title: Sextortion: what it is and exactly what to do

scenes.text: Aryan, 16, chatted with a 'girl' who sent a photo and asked for one back. He sent it.
Minutes later: 'Pay ₹10,000 or I send this to your family and school.' He panics and wants to pay.
He tells his elder brother. They don't pay, save evidence, report to 1930 and the platform. The account is removed. Aryan learns: this happens to many, and it's not his fault.

steps.title: What sextortion is
steps.body: **Sextortion** is when someone threatens to share intimate images (real, stolen or **fake/AI-made**) unless you pay money, send more images or do something. Often run by organised scam groups using fake profiles, targeting teen boys for money and others for more images. It is a crime.

steps.title: Exactly what to do
steps.body:
1. **Stop replying.** Don't argue or negotiate.
2. **Don't pay** — payment usually leads to more demands, not deletion.
3. **Save evidence**: screenshots of profile, chats, usernames, payment requests, links.
4. **Report & block** on the platform (after saving evidence).
5. **Report to police**: **cybercrime.gov.in** or call **1930** (national cybercrime helpline); **112** if in danger; **1098** if under 18.
6. **Get images removed**: under-18 → Take It Down; 18+ → StopNCII; platform reporting tools.
7. **Tell a trusted adult** — you are not in trouble for asking for help.
8. Tighten privacy; tell close friends not to engage if contacted.

steps.title: You are not alone
steps.body: People who are targeted often feel intense panic and shame. **It is not your fault — the criminal is responsible.** If you feel hopeless or have thoughts of harming yourself, please talk to someone right away: **Tele-MANAS 14416** or **112**. This situation can be handled.

steps.title: Solved example: the evidence list
steps.body: Save: (1) profile name & link, (2) user IDs/phone numbers, (3) chat screenshots with dates, (4) payment details asked (UPI ID, account), (5) any links. Then block. Write a short timeline: when contact began, what was sent, when threats started.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Paying 'just once'.
- Deleting everything before saving evidence.
- Facing it alone.
- Believing the threat to 'send to everyone' is always carried out — often it isn't, especially once you stop engaging and report.

items: Report and block on the platform
Tell a trusted adult and use takedown tools

quiz.q: If threatened with an image, first:
quiz.why: If threatened with an image, stop replying and don't pay. Paying or sending more only encourages the blackmailer.
The national cybercrime helpline is 1930. 1098 is Childline, 14416 is Tele-MANAS and 100 is police.
Paying usually leads to more demands, because blackmailers see it works. It doesn't bring a refund, deletion or safety.
Before blocking, save evidence such as screenshots and usernames. It helps police act later.
Sextortion can use real, stolen or fake (AI-made) images. So even a fake can be used to threaten, and the victim is still not to blame.

lessons.title: Deepfakes, cyber-harassment and being an upstander online

scenes.text: A classmate uses an app to create a fake image of Meher and shares it.
Meher is devastated though it isn't even real.
Her friends refuse to share it, report it, and support her as she tells the principal and files a cyber complaint.

steps.title: Deepfakes & morphing
steps.body: AI tools can create fake images, videos or voices. Making or sharing sexual or humiliating fakes of someone is harassment and can be an offence (IT Act provisions, BNS, and POCSO if the person is under 18). Signs of fakes: odd lighting, blurry edges, unnatural blinking or lip-sync. Treat any 'shocking' clip with doubt.

steps.title: Be an upstander online
steps.body:
- **Don't like, comment or forward** harmful content.
- **Report** the post/account.
- **Support** the target privately: 'I saw that. Are you OK? I've reported it.'
- **Tell an adult** if it's serious.
- **Document** if the target asks for help.

steps.title: Solved example: how sharing multiplies harm
steps.body: If one person shares to 5 people and each of those shares to 5 more, after 3 rounds: 5 + 25 + 125 = **155 people**. One 'no' at the start stops it.

steps.title: General education
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice. Reporting: platform tools, **cybercrime.gov.in**, **1930**, school authorities.

a.text: A morphed embarrassing image of a classmate lands in your group chat. People are reacting with laughing emojis.

choices.label: Don't react; report it; message the classmate privately to support
Forward it to another group
choices.feedback: That multiplies harm and may be an offence.

x.text: It's spreading fast. You feel uneasy. What now?

choices.label: Delete your forward, report, and tell an adult

b.text: Your classmate replies, 'Thanks. I don't know what to do.'

choices.label: Offer to go with them to a teacher and help report at cybercrime.gov.in/1930
Tell them to ignore it

courses.title: Bullying, cyberbullying & ragging: targets, bystanders and change
courses.summary: What bullying is (and isn't), its forms including cyberbullying, what to do if you're targeted, how bystanders can become upstanders, help for those who bully to change, and ragging in colleges with Indian rules and helplines.
outcomes: Learners can define bullying and distinguish it from conflict
Learners can use safe responses and document bullying
Learners can act as upstanders using the 5 Ds
Learners who bully can understand why and how to change
Learners can describe anti-ragging rules and how to report
courses.guardianNote: Covers bullying, cyberbullying and college ragging from the viewpoint of targets, bystanders and those who bully, with practical scripts, reporting routes (school, UGC anti-ragging helpline 1800-180-5522, 1930, 1098) and emotional support. Non-graphic.

lessons.title: What bullying is — and what it isn't

scenes.text: For months, a group calls Sameer 'Chotu', hides his bag and laughs when he trips.
Teachers think it's 'just teasing'.
When Sameer's diary of incidents reaches the counsellor, she recognises a pattern — and acts.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body: **Bullying** is **repeated** behaviour **intended to hurt**, where there's an **imbalance of power** (size, age, popularity, numbers, information). One-off arguments between equals are **conflict**, not bullying — though they still matter.

steps.title: Forms
steps.body:
- **Physical**: hitting, pushing, damaging things.
- **Verbal**: name-calling, insults, threats, slurs about caste, religion, region, skin colour, disability, gender or body.
- **Social/relational**: excluding, spreading rumours, humiliating.
- **Cyber**: hurtful messages, embarrassing posts, fake accounts, exclusion from groups, sharing private info or images.
- **Sexual**: sexual comments, gestures, touching.

steps.title: Solved example: bullying or conflict?
steps.body:
(a) Two friends argue over a cricket score once → **conflict**.
(b) A group posts mocking memes about one student every week → **bullying (cyber)**: repeated, intent, power of numbers.
(c) A senior forces a junior to hand over lunch daily → **bullying (physical/extortion)**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'It's just a joke' — if it repeatedly hurts and they can't make it stop, it's not.
- 'Toughen up' — bullying harms mental health and learning.
- Labelling a child 'a bully' forever — behaviour can change.

items.text: Weekly mocking memes about one student
Two friends disagree about a film
A group excludes one child every day
One argument in a match, then they make up

quiz.why: Bullying is repeated, intended to hurt and involves a power imbalance. One disagreement, friendly jokes and sport are not bullying.
Spreading rumours is social (relational) bullying, because it harms someone's friendships and reputation. It is not just conflict.
Fake accounts used to mock someone are cyberbullying, because they use technology to hurt. It is not legal fun or harmless.

quiz.q: 'It's just a joke' when it repeatedly hurts:
quiz.why: If a 'joke' repeatedly hurts, it is not acceptable. Impact on the other person matters more than the intent.
Yes, behaviour can change with support, understanding and effort. People who bully can learn better ways.

scenes.text: Lina starts a diary: date, what happened, who saw, how she felt.
She shows it to her mother and the class teacher.
The school meets the students involved and parents; the behaviour stops within weeks.

steps.title: In the moment
steps.body:
- Stay calm if you can; use a firm, short line: 'Stop. Not okay.' Then **walk away** to people or adults.
- Don't fight back physically (you could get hurt or blamed).
- Use humour or agree-and-move-on ('Maybe. Anyway…') if it feels safe.
- Stick near friends; avoid isolated spots.

steps.title: After: document and tell
steps.body: Keep a record (date, place, what, who saw). Save screenshots of online bullying (with usernames and dates). Tell a parent, teacher, counsellor or principal. Schools in India are expected to have anti-bullying measures (CBSE has issued anti-bullying guidelines). If it doesn't stop, **escalate** — principal, school management, and for serious cases, police / **1098** (under-18) / **1930** (cyber).

steps.title: Solved example: a complaint note
steps.body: 'On 3, 5 and 9 Oct, in the canteen, Rahul and Vivek took my lunch and called me names. Aman saw on 5 Oct. On 9 Oct they posted a photo of me with a mocking caption (screenshot attached). I feel scared to go to the canteen. Please help stop this.'

steps.title: Look after yourself
steps.body: It is **not your fault**. Spend time with people who treat you well; keep doing what you enjoy. If you feel very low, can't sleep, or think about hurting yourself — talk to someone now: **14416**.

activity.prompt: If bullying happened to you, who are the two adults you'd tell first, and what would you write in your first diary entry?
activity.hint: Date, place, what happened, who saw, how you felt.

options: firm line, walk away to people
quiz.why: The best immediate response is to say a firm line and walk away to other people. Crying alone, fighting or posting revenge can make things worse.
Document the date, place, what happened, witnesses and screenshots. Clear facts help adults act.
If the school doesn't stop it, escalate to the principal, management or higher authority. Giving up or fighting won't solve it.
Keep screenshots showing usernames and dates as evidence. Replying angrily, forwarding or deleting everything weakens your case.
No. Being bullied is never your fault; the person bullying is responsible.

lessons.title: Bystanders to upstanders — and changing bullying behaviour

scenes.text: Every day a group mocks Pranav's accent at lunch. Ten classmates watch silently.
One day Diya says, 'Come sit with us, Pranav.' Two others join.
Without an audience, the mocking fades. 'Bullying needs an audience,' says the teacher.

steps.title: The 5 Ds for bystanders
steps.body:
- **Direct**: 'Stop, that's not funny.' (if safe)
- **Distract**: change the subject; invite the target away.
- **Delegate**: get a teacher or adult.
- **Delay**: check in with the target afterwards.
- **Document**: note or screenshot (for online), give it to the target or an adult.

steps.title: If you've bullied someone
steps.body: People bully for many reasons: to fit in, feel powerful, copy what happens to them, deal with anger or stress at home, or not realising the harm. **You can change.** Steps: notice the urge and the trigger; pause; apologise sincerely ('I was wrong to…'); repair; find better ways to feel strong (sport, skills, leadership); talk to a counsellor about what's going on for you.

steps.title: Solved example: a real apology
steps.body:
Weak: 'Sorry if you felt bad.'
Strong: 'I'm sorry I called you names and shared that meme. It was wrong and hurtful. I've deleted it and I won't do it again. Is there anything I can do to make it right?'

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Laughing along 'to stay safe' — it fuels the bully.
- Thinking the target must 'stand up for themselves' alone.
- Bystanders posting the video 'as proof' publicly — give it to adults instead.

activity.prompt: Match the D to the action
pairs: Invite the target to join your game
Check in with the target later
Screenshot and give it to an adult

quiz.why: Bullying often depends on an audience, because people who bully want attention or approval. Without an audience it often loses its reward.
Delegate means getting an adult to help. It is a safe way to act when direct action is risky.
A strong apology names the specific wrong, repairs the harm and commits to change. Excuses, blame or 'sorry if you felt bad' are not real apologies.
People who bully can change with support. Punishment alone doesn't always help, and ignoring it lets harm continue.
Laughing along fuels bullying, because it gives the person bullying the audience they want. It doesn't help the target.

lessons.title: Ragging in colleges: rules, rights and reporting

scenes.text: In his first week at an engineering hostel, Faraz is woken at 2 am by seniors for an 'intro'.
They make him do humiliating tasks and threaten to 'boycott' him.
Next day he calls the National Anti-Ragging Helpline. The anti-ragging squad acts; the seniors are suspended.

steps.title: Ragging is banned
steps.body: Ragging — any act by students that teases, humiliates, intimidates, physically or mentally harms, or forces a fresher to do something against their will — is **prohibited**. The **UGC Regulations on Curbing the Menace of Ragging in Higher Educational Institutions, 2009** (following Supreme Court directions) require every college to have an **Anti-Ragging Committee and Squad**, and students and parents to submit anti-ragging undertakings. Punishments range from suspension, hostel expulsion and withholding results to rustication and police action. Many states also have anti-ragging laws, and acts of violence or intimidation are offences under the BNS.

steps.title: How to report
steps.body:
- **National Anti-Ragging Helpline: 1800-180-5522** (toll-free, 24×7) and the official anti-ragging portal.
- College anti-ragging committee/squad, warden, dean, principal.
- Police / **112** in danger.
- Complaints can be made **confidentially**.

steps.title: Solved example: 'harmless intro' or ragging?
steps.body:
(a) Seniors organise an official welcome event with faculty → **fine**.
(b) Forcing juniors to sing at 2 am, strip, drink, do push-ups, or hand over money → **ragging — report**.
(c) Seniors offer optional mentoring and notes → **fine**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'It builds bonding / it's tradition' — the law says otherwise.
- Fearing seniors' boycott — institutions must protect complainants.
- Seniors: 'It happened to us' is not a defence.

options: Escalate to principal/management; for serious threats, police/1098
questions.why: Escalate to the principal or management, and involve the police or 1098 for serious threats. Giving up, posting names online or retaliating doesn't solve it.

questions.why: Under UGC rules, ragging can lead to punishments such as suspension, hostel expulsion and rustication. It is not rewarded.

options: Support him to get help and change behaviour, while stopping the bullying

courses.title: How addiction works — and alcohol in depth
courses.summary: The brain science of addiction in plain words, the spectrum from use to dependence, alcohol's health effects, dangerous withdrawal, and treatment options.
outcomes: Explain addiction as a treatable brain-and-behaviour condition
Recognise harmful drinking and dependence

courses.guardianNote: Adults-only (18+) course: medically accurate, non-explicit and judgment-free health education.

lessons.title: Addiction is not a moral failing

scenes.text: Mohan, 52, promised many times to stop drinking and failed.
The family calls him weak.
A doctor explains addiction changes brain reward and control systems.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor, pharmacist or qualified counsellor. In an emergency call **112**. Mental health support: **Tele-MANAS 14416** (free, 24×7).

steps.title: What happens in the brain
steps.body: Substances and some behaviours strongly activate the brain's reward (dopamine) system. With repeated use the brain adapts: **tolerance** (needing more), **withdrawal** (feeling ill without it), **craving**, and weakened self-control circuits.

steps.title: Risk factors
steps.body: Genes, early first use, trauma, mental-health conditions, stress, availability, and peer and family patterns. It can happen to anyone.

steps.title: A treatable condition
steps.body: WHO and ICD-11 classify substance-use disorders as health conditions. Treatment — medicines, therapy, support groups — works, and relapse is part of many recovery journeys, not a reason to give up.

statements.s: Addiction is simply a lack of willpower.
statements.why: It involves brain changes and many risk factors.

statements.s: Tolerance means needing more for the same effect.
Relapse means treatment has failed forever.
Early first use raises addiction risk.
statements.why: The adolescent brain is more vulnerable.

options: Needing more for the same effect

lessons.title: Alcohol: harms, limits and red flags

scenes.text: Neha, 28, drinks heavily at weekend parties but 'never on weekdays'.
She blacks out twice in a month.
Her doctor uses the AUDIT questionnaire.

steps.title: No safe level
steps.body: WHO (2023) states there is no level of alcohol consumption that is safe for health. Risk rises with amount.

steps.title: Health effects
steps.body: Liver disease, several cancers (mouth, throat, oesophagus, liver, breast, bowel), high blood pressure, heart problems, pancreatitis, depression and anxiety, accidents, violence, and harm in pregnancy.

steps.title: Red flags
steps.body: Blackouts, drinking in the morning, failing to cut down, drinking to cope with feelings, others worried, binge drinking, drink-driving.

steps.title: Alcohol poisoning
steps.body: Confusion, vomiting while drowsy, slow or irregular breathing, cold clammy skin, unresponsiveness — call **112**, keep them on their side, never leave them alone. Do not give coffee or cold showers.

activity.prompt: Is it a red flag for problem drinking?
buckets: Not a red flag by itself

items.text: Drinking in the morning to feel normal
Choosing a soft drink at a party

options: Two drinks a day are healthy

quiz.q: Someone unresponsive after heavy drinking needs…

options: A screening questionnaire for alcohol use

scenes.text: Mohan decides to quit and plans to stop suddenly at home.
His doctor warns about withdrawal seizures.
He has supervised detox instead.

steps.title: Withdrawal can be dangerous
steps.body: In heavy, long-term drinkers, stopping suddenly can cause tremors, sweating, anxiety, seizures and **delirium tremens** (confusion, hallucinations) — potentially fatal. Detox should be medically supervised.

steps.title: Treatment options
steps.body: Medically supervised detox; medicines that reduce craving or relapse (e.g. naltrexone, acamprosate; disulfiram in selected cases — only on prescription); thiamine (vitamin B1) to protect the brain; counselling (motivational interviewing, CBT); mutual-help groups (e.g. AA, which has many groups in India).

steps.title: Government services
steps.body: Government de-addiction centres and many district hospitals offer treatment; call **14446**.

items.q: Can I just stop on my own?
items.a: If you drink heavily every day, don't stop suddenly without medical advice — withdrawal can cause seizures. Talk to a doctor first.

items.q: Is there medicine to help?
items.a: Yes, several prescribed medicines reduce craving or relapse.

items.q: What if I slip?
items.a: A slip is not failure. Tell your support person or doctor and continue.

items.q: Will rehab be like prison?
items.a: Good centres are voluntary and respectful. Under the MHCA 2017 you have rights to dignity. Avoid any centre that uses chains or violence.

steps.title: India's burden
steps.body: India has one of the world's largest populations of tobacco users, and smokeless tobacco is very common. Tobacco causes over a million deaths a year in India by commonly cited estimates.

steps.title: Smokeless tobacco harms
steps.body: Gutka, khaini, zarda and similar products cause mouth, throat and oesophageal cancers, gum disease, tooth loss, and pre-cancerous lesions (white/red patches, stiff mouth opening — oral submucous fibrosis).

steps.title: Smoking harms
steps.body: Lung and many other cancers, heart attack, stroke, COPD, TB risk, infertility, erectile problems, harm to babies. Bidis are not safer than cigarettes.

steps.title: See a dentist/doctor

steps.title: E-cigarettes in India
steps.body: The Prohibition of Electronic Cigarettes Act, 2019 bans the production, sale, import, distribution, storage and advertisement of e-cigarettes in India.

steps.title: COTPA 2003
steps.body: Prohibits smoking in public places, tobacco advertising, sale to people under 18 and near educational institutions, and requires health warnings. Many states have banned gutka under food-safety rules.

steps.title: Vaping health
steps.body: Most vapes contain nicotine, which is highly addictive; long-term effects are still being studied and products bought illegally may be contaminated. They are not a recommended quitting tool in India.

steps.title: What works best
steps.body: Combining **behavioural support** (counselling, quitline, apps) with **medicines** (nicotine replacement — gum, lozenges, patches; or prescribed medicines such as varenicline or bupropion) roughly doubles or triples success compared with willpower alone.

steps.title: Practical tips
steps.body: Set a quit date, remove tobacco from home and vehicle, identify triggers (tea, stress, after meals), find replacements (fennel/saunf, sugar-free gum, a walk), tell friends, and plan for cravings — they peak and pass within minutes.

steps.title: Benefits begin fast
steps.body: Within days carbon monoxide levels fall; within months breathing improves; over years risks of heart disease and cancer drop substantially.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor, pharmacist or qualified counsellor. In an emergency call **112**. Mental health support: **Tele-MANAS 14416** (free, 24×7).

steps.title: Effects
steps.body: Relaxation, altered perception, increased appetite; also anxiety, paranoia, impaired memory and coordination. Edibles (including bhang) act slowly and unpredictably — people often take too much.

steps.title: Risks
steps.body: About 1 in 10 users develop cannabis use disorder (higher with daily, early use). Regular high-potency use raises psychosis and schizophrenia risk, especially with family history. Driving under the influence raises crash risk.

steps.title: Law in general terms
steps.body: Under the NDPS Act 1985, cultivation, possession, sale and use of ganja (flowering tops) and charas (resin) are offences. Bhang (leaves) is regulated by states. This is general education, not legal advice.

steps.title: Cutting down
steps.body: Track use, set use-free days, avoid triggers, get support. Withdrawal (irritability, poor sleep, vivid dreams) usually settles within about two weeks.

statements.s: Cannabis can't be addictive.
statements.why: Cannabis use disorder is well recognised.

statements.s: Daily high-potency use raises psychosis risk.

scenes.text: Gurpreet finds his cousin unresponsive with pinpoint pupils and slow breathing.
He calls 112.

steps.title: What opioids are
steps.body: Heroin ('smack', 'brown sugar'), morphine, codeine (some cough syrups), tramadol, and other painkillers. They relieve pain but cause tolerance, dependence and can stop breathing in overdose.

steps.title: Signs of opioid overdose
steps.body: Unresponsive or hard to wake, slow/shallow/stopped breathing, blue lips, pinpoint pupils, gurgling sounds. **Call 112 immediately**, try to wake them, put them in the recovery position, give naloxone if available and trained, and start CPR if not breathing.

steps.title: Naloxone
steps.body: A medicine that temporarily reverses opioid overdose. It wears off sooner than many opioids, so medical care is still needed.

steps.title: Mixing raises risk
steps.body: Combining opioids with alcohol or sleeping pills (benzodiazepines) greatly increases overdose risk. Tolerance drops after a break (e.g. after rehab or jail) — overdose risk is very high on return.

activity.prompt: Order the steps when you find a possible opioid overdose
