quiz.q: Overdose risk is very high after a break because…

lessons.title: Treatment: OST, rehab and harm reduction

scenes.text: Gurpreet's cousin starts buprenorphine at a government OST centre.
Six months later he's working again.
He attends counselling weekly.

steps.title: Opioid substitution therapy (OST)
steps.body: Supervised long-acting medicines such as **buprenorphine** or **methadone** reduce craving and withdrawal, cut overdose deaths and HIV/hepatitis spread, and help people rebuild lives. It's evidence-based treatment, not 'swapping one drug for another'.

steps.title: Other care
steps.body: Detox, counselling, family therapy, rehabilitation, treatment of mental-health conditions, and needle-syringe programmes for people who inject (to prevent HIV and hepatitis C).

steps.title: Choose ethical centres
steps.body: Avoid unlicensed 'rehabs' that use force, chains or beatings — these are illegal and harmful. Ask for licensed, doctor-led services; call 14446.

items.q: Isn't OST just another addiction?
items.a: No. Prescribed, supervised medicine stabilises the brain, and outcomes (deaths, crime, HIV) are much better than without it.

items.q: Will the police arrest my son if he seeks treatment?
items.a: The NDPS Act provides that people with addiction who volunteer for treatment can be eligible for immunity from prosecution under certain conditions. Ask a lawyer for specifics.

items.q: How long is treatment?
items.a: Often months to years — like other chronic conditions.

items.q: Can he still work?
items.a: Yes, many people on OST work and support families.

steps.title: Signs
steps.body: Chasing losses, betting more for the same thrill, lying about gambling, borrowing or stealing to gamble, restlessness when trying to stop, gambling to escape problems. Gambling disorder is a recognised mental-health condition.

steps.title: Why it hooks
steps.body: Unpredictable rewards and 'near misses' strongly activate reward circuits. Apps add 24×7 access, bonuses and notifications.

steps.title: Practical steps
steps.body: Self-exclude and delete apps, use bank gambling blocks where available, hand over financial control temporarily, avoid instant-loan apps, and talk to someone. Debt can be addressed with honest planning and, if needed, a financial counsellor.

steps.title: Suicide risk
steps.body: Problem gambling and debt are linked to higher suicide risk. If you feel hopeless, call 14416 or 112.

steps.title: Use vs compulsion
steps.body: Many adults view porn without problems. It becomes a concern when it's out of control, causes distress, harms work or relationships, or continues despite wanting to stop. ICD-11 includes **compulsive sexual behaviour disorder**.

steps.title: Shame doesn't help
steps.body: Moral shame often deepens the cycle. Therapy (CBT, acceptance-based approaches) focuses on triggers, emotions, and values.

steps.title: Practical steps
steps.body: Notice triggers (boredom, stress, loneliness, late-night phone), use blockers and keep devices out of the bedroom, build other coping (exercise, connection, sleep), and talk honestly with a partner or therapist.

steps.title: Illegal content
steps.body: Child sexual abuse material is a serious crime under POCSO and the IT Act. If you're worried about your thoughts or urges, seek professional help confidentially.

steps.title: ICD-11 definition
steps.body: Gaming disorder: impaired control over gaming, increasing priority over other activities, and continuing despite harm — usually for at least 12 months, with significant impairment. Most gamers don't have it.

steps.title: Balance
steps.body: Set time limits and gaming-free zones, keep sleep and meals regular, schedule offline activities, and watch for gaming used to escape anxiety or depression.

steps.title: Treatment
steps.body: CBT, family therapy, treating underlying anxiety/depression/ADHD. Sudden harsh bans often backfire; agreed, gradual plans work better.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor, pharmacist or qualified counsellor. In an emergency call **112**. Mental health support: **Tele-MANAS 14416** (free, 24×7).

steps.title: How conception happens
steps.body: An egg lives about 12–24 hours after ovulation; sperm can survive up to about 5 days. So the fertile window is about **6 days**: the 5 days before ovulation plus ovulation day.

steps.title: Ovulation timing
steps.body: Ovulation usually happens about 14 days *before* the next period, not 14 days after the last one. In a 35-day cycle that's around day 21.

steps.title: Practical approach
steps.body: Having sex every 2–3 days through the cycle covers the window without stress. Ovulation kits (LH tests) and cervical-mucus changes can help pinpoint it.

steps.title: Don't over-track
steps.body: Constant timing can create pressure for both partners. Regular intimacy is usually enough.

statements.s: The fertile window is about 6 days.
Everyone ovulates on day 14.
Sex every 2–3 days covers the fertile window.
An egg survives about a week.

quiz.q: In a 35-day cycle, ovulation is likely around…
quiz.why: About 14 days before the next period.

quiz.q: How long can sperm survive in the reproductive tract?
quiz.why: That's why the window starts before ovulation.

quiz.q: A low-stress approach to trying is…

scenes.text: Arjun and Divya plan to start trying in three months.
They ask what they can do now.
Their doctor starts Divya on folic acid and asks Arjun to cut smoking.

steps.title: For the person who will be pregnant
steps.body: Folic acid (commonly 400 micrograms daily, started before conception) lowers the risk of neural-tube defects. Check rubella immunity, thyroid, blood sugar, anaemia and medicines.

steps.title: For partners producing sperm
steps.body: Sperm take around 2–3 months to develop, so changes now matter: stop smoking, limit alcohol, avoid anabolic steroids and testosterone supplements (which suppress sperm production), avoid frequent hot baths or laptops on the lap, keep a healthy weight.

steps.title: Shared factors
steps.body: Smoking, heavy alcohol, obesity or very low weight, uncontrolled diabetes, and some STIs reduce fertility in both sexes.

steps.title: Age
steps.body: Female fertility declines gradually from the early 30s and faster after about 35; male fertility also declines with age, more slowly.

items: Start folic acid before trying (if you will be pregnant)
Review all regular medicines with a doctor
Check rubella and hepatitis B status
Stop smoking/tobacco and cut alcohol (both partners)
Aim for a healthy weight and regular activity

quiz.q: Folic acid before conception reduces risk of…

quiz.why: They suppress the body's own signals.

lessons.title: When to seek help, and myths

scenes.text: Sunita, 31, and Ravi have tried for 13 months.

steps.title: When to see a doctor
steps.body: Usually after **12 months** of regular unprotected sex if under 35, after **6 months** if 35 or over, or sooner with irregular/absent periods, known endometriosis or PCOS, previous pelvic infection, or known male factors.

steps.title: It's not only the woman

steps.title: Myths
steps.body: Lying with legs up, specific positions, or particular foods don't meaningfully change conception odds. Stress doesn't 'cause' infertility in a simple way, though looking after mental health matters.

steps.title: How common
steps.body: WHO estimates about 1 in 6 people worldwide experience infertility in their lifetime.

steps.title: Female causes
steps.body: Ovulation problems (PCOS, thyroid, high prolactin, very low/high weight), blocked tubes (past infections, including untreated chlamydia/gonorrhoea, genital TB in India), endometriosis, fibroids or polyps, age-related decline in egg number and quality.

steps.title: Male causes
steps.body: Low count or motility, blockages, varicocele, hormone problems, genetic causes, infections, smoking, heat, steroid use, some medicines.

steps.title: Unexplained
steps.body: In a portion of couples, standard tests are normal — this is 'unexplained infertility', and treatments still help.

lessons.title: IUI and IVF step by step

scenes.text: Leela and Tom visit an ART clinic.
The doctor outlines IUI, then IVF if needed.

steps.title: IUI (intrauterine insemination)
steps.body: Prepared sperm are placed into the uterus around ovulation, often with mild ovulation medicines. Simpler and cheaper; useful for mild male factor, cervical factors, unexplained infertility or donor sperm.

steps.title: IVF (in vitro fertilisation)
steps.body: 1) Ovarian stimulation with injections and scans. 2) Egg collection under sedation. 3) Eggs fertilised in the lab (ICSI = one sperm injected into each egg, used for male factor). 4) Embryos grow for a few days. 5) Embryo transfer into the uterus. 6) Pregnancy test about two weeks later. Extra embryos may be frozen.

steps.title: Success depends heavily on age
steps.body: Success per cycle is highest in younger women and falls with age. Ask clinics for their age-specific results, not just headline numbers.

steps.title: Regulation in India
steps.body: The Assisted Reproductive Technology (Regulation) Act, 2021 and the Surrogacy (Regulation) Act, 2021 regulate clinics, banks and surrogacy. Sex selection is illegal under the PCPNDT Act. This is general education, not legal advice.

steps.title: Risks
steps.body: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome, multiple pregnancy, and emotional/financial strain. Clinics should counsel you on each.

steps.title: PCOS (polycystic ovary syndrome)
steps.body: A common hormonal condition. Diagnosis (Rotterdam criteria) needs **2 of 3**: irregular or absent ovulation, signs of high androgens (acne, excess hair, or blood tests), and polycystic-appearing ovaries on ultrasound — after excluding other causes.

steps.title: Managing PCOS
steps.body: Healthy lifestyle (even 5–10% weight loss helps if overweight), treatment for periods and skin, metformin in some cases, ovulation-induction medicines when trying to conceive. Monitor diabetes, cholesterol and mood risk. Many people with PCOS do conceive.

steps.title: Endometriosis
steps.body: Tissue similar to the uterine lining grows outside the uterus, causing painful periods, pain with sex, pelvic pain, bowel/bladder pain and sometimes infertility. WHO estimates it affects about 10% of reproductive-age women and girls. Diagnosis is often delayed by years.

steps.title: Period pain that stops your life is not 'normal'
steps.body: Pain that doesn't respond to usual painkillers or causes missed school/work deserves assessment by a gynaecologist.

steps.title: Dating
steps.body: Pregnancy is counted from the first day of the last menstrual period; a full-term pregnancy is about 40 weeks. Early ultrasound refines dating.

steps.title: Trimesters in general terms
steps.body:
- **First (weeks 1–13)**: organs form; nausea and tiredness are common.
- **Second (14–27)**: energy often returns; movements are usually felt around 18–22 weeks; anomaly scan around 18–22 weeks.
- **Third (28–40)**: rapid growth; baby's position checked; birth planning.

steps.title: Antenatal care
steps.body: Regular check-ups (WHO recommends at least 8 contacts), blood pressure, weight, blood and urine tests, iron and folic acid, tetanus-diphtheria vaccination, screening for HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B, diabetes and anaemia.

steps.title: Sex determination is illegal
steps.body: Under the PCPNDT Act it is illegal to determine or disclose the sex of the fetus in India.

steps.title: Common and usually not anyone's fault
steps.body: Miscarriage ends roughly 10–20% of known pregnancies, mostly in the first trimester, and most are caused by chromosomal problems in the embryo. Everyday activities, work, sex, mild stress or eating papaya are not usual causes.

steps.title: Medical care
steps.body: Bleeding and cramping need assessment to confirm what's happening and rule out ectopic pregnancy (a pregnancy outside the uterus — an emergency with severe one-sided pain, fainting or shoulder-tip pain). Management may be waiting, medicines or a minor procedure.

steps.title: Recurrent loss
steps.body: Two or three or more losses deserve specialist evaluation; some causes are treatable.

steps.title: Supporting someone
steps.body: Say 'I'm so sorry'. Use the words they use. Don't say 'at least it was early' or 'you can try again'. Partners grieve too. Grief can return around due dates.

items.q: Did I cause it?
items.a: Almost always no. Most early losses are due to chromosomal problems that couldn't be prevented.

items.q: When can we try again?
items.a: Many people can try after their next period if physically and emotionally ready — ask your doctor.

items.q: Is it normal to grieve this much?
items.a: Yes. Grief after loss at any stage is real. Counselling helps; Tele-MANAS 14416 is free.

items.q: What is an ectopic pregnancy?
items.a: A pregnancy outside the uterus, usually in a tube. Severe one-sided pain or fainting is an emergency — call 112.

lessons.title: The MTP Act as amended in 2021 — in general terms

scenes.text: Rashmi, 27, unmarried, is 8 weeks pregnant and doesn't want to continue.
She has heard abortion is illegal for unmarried women.
A government hospital doctor explains the law.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor, pharmacist or qualified counsellor. In an emergency call **112**. Mental health support: **Tele-MANAS 14416** (free, 24×7).

steps.title: Legal and safe
steps.body: In India, abortion by a registered medical practitioner under the MTP Act is legal on defined grounds, including risk to the woman's physical or mental health, fetal abnormality, and contraceptive failure.

steps.title: Gestational limits (general terms)
steps.body:
- **Up to 20 weeks**: on the opinion of one registered medical practitioner.
- **20–24 weeks**: for specified categories (such as survivors of sexual assault, minors, change in marital status, women with disabilities, and others listed in the rules), on the opinion of two practitioners.
- **Beyond 24 weeks**: in cases of substantial fetal abnormalities, on the decision of a state-level Medical Board.

steps.title: Unmarried women
steps.body: The 2021 amendment extended the contraceptive-failure ground to 'any woman or her partner', and in 2022 the Supreme Court held that unmarried women are equally entitled to safe abortion under the Act.

steps.title: Confidentiality
steps.body: The Act requires the woman's identity to be kept confidential. An adult woman's consent is required; a husband's or family's consent is not legally required for an adult.

steps.title: Unsafe abortion kills
steps.body: Avoid unqualified providers and unprescribed pills. Medical abortion pills must be prescribed and supervised by a registered doctor. This is general education, not legal advice.

statements.s: Abortion in India is legal on defined grounds under the MTP Act.
Unmarried women cannot legally access abortion.
statements.why: The 2021 amendment and 2022 Supreme Court ruling include them.

statements.s: An adult woman needs her husband's consent by law.
statements.why: Her own consent is what's required.

statements.s: Up to 20 weeks, one registered doctor's opinion is required.

quiz.q: Upper limit for specified categories under the amended Act?

quiz.why: Changed from 'married woman or her husband'.

steps.title: Options in general terms
steps.body: Early pregnancies can often be ended with medicines prescribed and supervised by a doctor, or by a short procedure (vacuum aspiration). Later pregnancies need different methods in an approved facility.

steps.title: When to seek urgent care after an abortion
steps.body: Heavy bleeding (soaking more than two thick pads an hour for two hours), fever, foul-smelling discharge, severe pain or fainting — go to hospital or call 112.

steps.title: Aftercare
steps.body: Fertility can return within weeks — start contraception soon. Emotional reactions vary: relief, sadness, both. Counselling is available; Tele-MANAS 14416.

steps.title: Minors
steps.body: For someone under 18, a guardian's consent is required and medical staff have reporting duties under POCSO. Services remain available — seek help from a doctor or Childline 1098.

activity.prompt: Questions people are scared to ask

items.q: Will an abortion make me infertile?
items.a: A safe, legal abortion does not usually affect future fertility. Unsafe abortions can cause damage — that's why safe care matters.

items.q: Will my family find out?
items.a: The law requires confidentiality for adult women.

items.q: Is it a sin / am I a bad person?
items.a: People hold many beliefs. Medically and legally, it's a health decision that belongs to you. Counselling can help you process feelings.

items.q: Can I get contraception at the same visit?
items.a: Yes — many methods can start the same day.

steps.title: Baby blues
steps.body: Very common in the first days after birth: tearfulness, mood swings. Usually settles within about 2 weeks.

steps.title: Postpartum depression (PPD)
steps.body: Low mood, loss of interest, anxiety, guilt, sleep and appetite changes, difficulty bonding, or thoughts of harming oneself lasting more than 2 weeks, starting in pregnancy or the year after birth. It's common — affecting roughly 1 in 7 to 1 in 5 new mothers in many studies — and treatable with support, talking therapy, and medicines (many compatible with breastfeeding). Fathers and partners can also develop depression.

steps.title: Postpartum psychosis is an emergency
steps.body: Rare but serious: confusion, hallucinations, extreme mood changes, paranoid thoughts, usually in the first weeks. Call **112** or go to hospital the same day.

steps.title: How family can help
steps.body: Share night feeds and chores, let her sleep, listen without judgment, go with her to the doctor.

outcomes: Define perimenopause and menopause

scenes.text: Rekha, 47, wakes drenched in sweat and forgets words in meetings.
She fears early dementia.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor, pharmacist or qualified counsellor. In an emergency call **112**. Mental health support: **Tele-MANAS 14416** (free, 24×7).

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: **Menopause** = 12 months in a row without a period (not due to another cause). **Perimenopause** = the years before, when hormones fluctuate. In India, menopause often happens in the mid-to-late 40s; globally the average is around 51. Before 40 is 'premature ovarian insufficiency' and needs evaluation.

steps.title: Common symptoms
steps.body: Irregular periods, hot flushes and night sweats, sleep problems, mood changes, brain fog, joint aches, vaginal dryness, urinary urgency, lower desire.

steps.title: Bleeding after menopause
steps.body: Any bleeding after 12 months without periods must be checked by a doctor promptly.

steps.title: Contraception
steps.body: Pregnancy is still possible in perimenopause — continue contraception until your doctor advises (commonly until 12 months after the last period if over 50).

statements.s: Menopause is confirmed after 12 months without a period.
Brain fog in perimenopause means dementia.
Bleeding after menopause should be checked.
Pregnancy is impossible in perimenopause.

quiz.q: Night sweats are typically due to…

lessons.title: Treatment: HRT, non-hormonal options, bone & heart

scenes.text: Rekha's doctor discusses hormone therapy.
She's read HRT 'causes cancer'.
They weigh benefits and risks for her.

steps.title: HRT (menopausal hormone therapy)
steps.body: The most effective treatment for hot flushes and night sweats. People with a uterus need a progestogen with oestrogen to protect the womb lining. Benefits/risks depend on age, time since menopause, and personal history; for many healthy women under 60 or within 10 years of menopause, benefits often outweigh risks.

steps.title: Risks in general terms
steps.body: Combined HRT is linked with a small increase in breast-cancer risk with longer use; tablets carry a small clot risk (patches/gels less so). Not suitable for some people with a history of certain cancers, clots or liver disease. Decide with your doctor.

steps.title: Non-hormonal options
steps.body: Lifestyle (cooling, layered clothing, limiting alcohol and caffeine), CBT for flushes and sleep, certain prescribed non-hormonal medicines, and vaginal moisturisers or local oestrogen for dryness.

steps.title: Bone and heart
steps.body: Oestrogen loss speeds bone loss. Weight-bearing exercise, calcium and vitamin D from diet (supplements if advised), no smoking, and bone-density testing when advised. Heart-disease risk rises — check BP, sugar and cholesterol.

items.q: Is HRT dangerous?
items.a: For many healthy women near menopause, benefits outweigh risks. It depends on your history — discuss it individually.

items.q: Will my sex life end?
items.a: No. Dryness and desire changes are treatable, and many enjoy intimacy for decades.

items.q: Why am I so angry or sad?
items.a: Hormone shifts affect mood. If low mood persists, talk to a doctor — treatment helps.

items.q: Do I need calcium tablets?
items.a: Diet first; your doctor may suggest supplements or a bone-density scan.

quiz.q: Most effective treatment for hot flushes?
Why add progestogen in HRT for women with a uterus?

scenes.text: Prakash, 55, feels tired, low and less interested in sex.

steps.title: Not a sudden 'male menopause'
steps.body: Testosterone declines gradually with age. 'Andropause' is better described as **late-onset hypogonadism** — low testosterone *plus* symptoms.

steps.title: Diagnosis
steps.body: Symptoms (low desire, fewer morning erections, fatigue, low mood, reduced muscle) AND low testosterone on morning blood tests, usually repeated. Obesity, diabetes, sleep apnoea, alcohol and some medicines lower testosterone and should be addressed.

steps.title: Testosterone isn't a tonic
steps.body: Unnecessary testosterone can stop sperm production, raise red-cell counts, and has other risks. Use only when prescribed after proper testing.

steps.title: Midlife men's health
steps.body: Check BP, sugar, cholesterol; discuss prostate symptoms; watch mood — depression in men often shows as irritability or withdrawal.

statements.s: Andropause is a sudden stop like menopause.
Low testosterone is diagnosed by symptoms plus repeated morning tests.
Testosterone injections can lower sperm production.
statements.why: They suppress the body's own signals.

statements.s: Weight loss and better sleep can raise testosterone.

courses.title: LGBTQ+ health & coming out
courses.summary: Sexual orientation facts, health needs of LGBTQ+ adults, Indian law in general terms, and how to come out — or support someone who does — safely.
outcomes: Use accurate, respectful terms
Describe LGBTQ+ health needs and minority stress
Know key legal milestones in India
Plan or support a safe coming-out

lessons.title: Orientation facts and respectful language

scenes.text: Aarav, 22, realises he's attracted to men and wonders if something is 'wrong'.
He reads WHO and medical sources.
He learns orientation is a normal variation.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor, pharmacist or qualified counsellor. In an emergency call **112**. Mental health support: **Tele-MANAS 14416** (free, 24×7).

steps.title: Terms
steps.body: **Sexual orientation**: who you're attracted to (e.g. lesbian, gay, bisexual, asexual, heterosexual). **Gender identity**: your inner sense of your gender. **Sex characteristics**: body features. These are separate.

steps.title: Not an illness
steps.body: Homosexuality was removed from WHO's disease classification decades ago. Major medical bodies agree orientation is not a disorder and cannot be 'cured'.

steps.title: Conversion therapy harms
steps.body: Attempts to change orientation or identity are ineffective and linked with depression and suicidality. India's National Medical Commission has declared conversion therapy professional misconduct (2022).

steps.title: Respect
steps.body: Use the words people use for themselves, ask pronouns politely, and avoid outing anyone.

statements.s: Sexual orientation and gender identity are the same thing.
Homosexuality is classified as a mental illness by WHO.
Conversion therapy is effective.
Outing someone without consent can put them at risk.

quiz.q: Is orientation a choice that can be cured?

sources: Navtej Singh Johar v Union of India 2018

lessons.title: Health needs and minority stress

scenes.text: Naina, 29, a lesbian, skips cervical screening because she assumes she doesn't need it.
Her doctor explains she does.

steps.title: Minority stress
steps.body: Stigma, discrimination and rejection increase rates of anxiety, depression, substance use and suicidal thoughts in LGBTQ+ people — not because of identity itself but because of how they're treated.

steps.title: Screening matters for everyone
steps.body: Women who have sex with women still need cervical screening; HPV can pass between partners. Men who have sex with men benefit from regular HIV/STI testing, hepatitis vaccination, and may benefit from PrEP.

steps.title: Affirming care
steps.body: Look for doctors who are non-judgmental; ask for confidentiality; bring a trusted person if you wish. Community organisations often keep lists of affirming clinicians.

items.q: Do lesbians need pap/HPV tests?
items.a: Yes. HPV can be transmitted between partners; follow normal screening guidance.

items.q: What is PrEP?
items.a: A medicine taken to prevent HIV for people at higher risk — prescribed and monitored by a doctor.

items.q: My family wants me to see a 'cure' doctor. What should I know?
items.a: Conversion therapy is harmful and doctors performing it commit professional misconduct (NMC 2022). You can refuse.

items.q: Is it normal to feel anxious all the time?
items.a: Minority stress is real. Supportive counselling helps; Tele-MANAS 14416 is free.

quiz.q: Do women who have sex with women need cervical screening?

sources: Navtej Singh Johar v Union of India 2018

steps.title: Legal milestones in general terms
steps.body:
- **2014 (NALSA)**: Supreme Court recognised transgender persons' right to self-identify gender.
- **2018 (Navtej Singh Johar)**: Supreme Court decriminalised consensual same-sex relations between adults.
- **2019**: Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act.
- **2023**: Supreme Court declined to legalise same-sex marriage, leaving it to Parliament. This is general education, not legal advice.

steps.title: Coming out is your choice
steps.body: There's no 'right' time. Consider: Are you safe (financially, physically)? Who is likely to be supportive? Do you have a plan if it goes badly?

steps.title: Supporting someone who comes out
steps.body: 'Thank you for trusting me.' Ask how you can support them, keep it confidential unless they say otherwise, and don't ask intrusive questions.

a.text: Aarav depends on his parents financially and they've made hostile comments. Safest first step?

choices.label: Tell a supportive person first and plan safety/finances
Tell everyone at the family dinner
Never tell anyone ever
choices.feedback: It's his choice, but support helps wellbeing.

b.text: His sister responds warmly. What should she do next?

choices.label: Thank him, keep it private and ask how she can help
Tell their parents herself

end.text: With his sister's support, Aarav plans the next steps at his own pace.

When someone comes out to you…

courses.title: Gender dysphoria, gender-affirming care & intersex facts
courses.summary: What gender incongruence and dysphoria are, what gender-affirming care involves in general terms, rights under the 2019 Act, and accurate, respectful facts about intersex variations.
outcomes: Define gender incongruence and dysphoria

lessons.title: Gender identity, incongruence and dysphoria

scenes.text: Riya, 24, assigned male at birth, has felt she is a woman since childhood.
She has felt intense distress about her body.
A psychiatrist explains gender dysphoria.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor, pharmacist or qualified counsellor. In an emergency call **112**. Mental health support: **Tele-MANAS 14416** (free, 24×7).

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: **Transgender**: gender identity differs from sex assigned at birth. **Non-binary**: identity outside man/woman. **Gender dysphoria**: distress that can come from this mismatch. Not all trans people experience severe dysphoria.

steps.title: ICD-11
steps.body: WHO's ICD-11 moved 'gender incongruence' out of the mental-disorders chapter into a sexual-health chapter — being trans is not a mental illness, but people may need health care.

steps.title: Mental health
steps.body: High rates of depression and suicidality among trans people are largely linked to stigma and rejection; family acceptance and affirming care are strongly protective.

statements.s: Being transgender is classified as a mental disorder in ICD-11.
Not all trans people experience severe dysphoria.
Family acceptance is protective for trans people's mental health.
Non-binary people identify outside man/woman.

options: Identity differs from sex assigned at birth

sources: Navtej Singh Johar v Union of India 2018

lessons.title: Gender-affirming care and legal rights

scenes.text: Riya meets an endocrinologist and a counsellor.
She applies for a transgender certificate on the national portal.
She chooses her own pace.

steps.title: Care in general terms
steps.body: Gender-affirming care is individual and can include social transition (name, clothes, pronouns), counselling, hormone therapy under specialist supervision, voice therapy, and for some adults, surgeries. Not everyone wants every step.

steps.title: Avoid unsupervised hormones
steps.body: Hormones bought without prescription can cause clots, liver problems and other harm. Seek an endocrinologist.

steps.title: Rights in general terms
steps.body: The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 prohibits discrimination in education, employment, health care and more, and provides for a certificate of identity via the District Magistrate. This is general education, not legal advice.

items.q: Does everyone have surgery?
items.a: No. Transition is personal; many people don't want or need surgery.

items.q: Can trans people have children?
items.a: Fertility may be affected by hormones; discussing fertility preservation before treatment is recommended.

items.q: Is it okay to ask about someone's surgery?
items.a: Generally no — it's private medical information, just as for anyone.

items.q: How do I apply for an identity certificate?
items.a: Through the government's National Portal for Transgender Persons, which routes to the District Magistrate.

quiz.q: Asking about someone's surgeries is usually…

sources: Navtej Singh Johar v Union of India 2018

lessons.title: Intersex facts

scenes.text: A baby is born with genitals that don't fit typical male/female categories.
The team explains intersex variations to the parents.
They avoid rushed decisions.

steps.title: What intersex means
steps.body: Intersex people are born with variations in sex characteristics (chromosomes, gonads, hormones or genitals) that don't fit typical binary definitions. Some are noticed at birth; others at puberty or later; some never.

steps.title: Examples
steps.body: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH), androgen insensitivity syndrome, Klinefelter syndrome (XXY), Turner syndrome and others. Prevalence estimates vary widely depending on definitions.

steps.title: Rights and care
steps.body: Human-rights bodies call for delaying medically unnecessary surgeries until the person can consent. In 2019 the Madras High Court directed a ban on sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants in Tamil Nadu. Some conditions (e.g. salt-wasting CAH) need urgent medical treatment.

steps.title: Language
steps.body: Intersex is about bodies, not identity — intersex people can have any gender identity or orientation.

statements.s: Intersex is the same as transgender.
Some intersex variations are discovered only at puberty or later.
Human-rights bodies call for delaying non-urgent surgeries.
Klinefelter syndrome (XXY) is an intersex variation.

quiz.q: Non-urgent genital surgery on infants is…

sources: Navtej Singh Johar v Union of India 2018

courses.title: Disability, sexuality & intimacy
courses.summary: People with disabilities have the same rights to love, intimacy and sexual health. Covers myths, practical adaptations, consent and capacity, abuse risks, and rights under the RPwD Act 2016.

lessons.title: Myths and rights

scenes.text: Sameera, 30, a wheelchair user, is getting married.
Relatives ask whether she 'can' have a sexual life or children.
She answers calmly.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor, pharmacist or qualified counsellor. In an emergency call **112**. Mental health support: **Tele-MANAS 14416** (free, 24×7).

steps.title: Myths
steps.body: People with disabilities are often assumed to be asexual, childlike or 'unable'. In reality they have the same range of desires, relationships and identities as anyone.

steps.title: Rights
steps.body: The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 (RPwD) guarantees equality and non-discrimination, and requires access to reproductive and sexual-health information and care. The UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities supports the right to marry and found a family.

steps.title: Ask, don't assume
steps.body: The person is the expert on their own body and needs.

statements.s: People with disabilities don't have sexual feelings.
The RPwD Act 2016 supports access to sexual and reproductive health care.
Many people with disabilities can have children.
statements.why: Depends on the person; ask a doctor.

statements.s: Asking the person directly is better than assuming.

quiz.q: The RPwD Act was passed in…
quiz.why: Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act.

quiz.q: Who is the expert on a disabled person's needs?
UN CRPD supports the right to…

lessons.title: Practical adaptations and help

scenes.text: Sameera and her husband talk with a rehabilitation doctor and occupational therapist.
They learn positioning, timing around fatigue and pain, and communication.

steps.title: Ideas that help
steps.body: Communication about what feels good and what hurts; positioning and pillows; timing around energy, pain medication or bladder/bowel routines; adaptive aids; exploring broader intimacy.

steps.title: Who helps
steps.body: Rehabilitation (PM&R) doctors, occupational therapists, physiotherapists, urologists (e.g. erection or ejaculation issues after spinal cord injury), gynaecologists, and counsellors.

steps.title: Health checks
steps.body: Contraception, STI prevention and cancer screening apply equally. Accessible clinics and information formats (sign language, easy-read, Braille) are rights under RPwD.

activity.prompt: Questions people with disabilities and partners ask

items.q: Can someone with a spinal cord injury have sex or children?
items.a: Many can, with adaptations and sometimes medical help (including fertility treatment). A rehabilitation specialist can advise.

items.q: What if a disability causes pain?
items.a: Plan timing around pain relief, try positions that reduce strain, and talk to a physiotherapist.

items.q: Do people with intellectual disabilities need sexuality education?
items.a: Yes — accessible education reduces abuse risk and supports healthy relationships.

items.q: Is it okay to ask a doctor about sex?
items.a: Absolutely — it's part of health.

quiz.q: Who can advise on positioning and aids?

lessons.title: Consent, capacity and protection from abuse

scenes.text: Arjun, 26, with an intellectual disability, has a girlfriend.
His parents worry about consent and safety.

steps.title: Consent and capacity
steps.body: Consent requires understanding and free choice. Many people with disabilities can consent; supported decision-making helps them understand and decide, rather than others deciding for them.

steps.title: Higher abuse risk
steps.body: People with disabilities face higher rates of sexual abuse, often by people they know. Accessible education, trusted reporting routes and believing disclosures are vital. Report abuse to 112.

steps.title: Forced sterilisation is a rights violation
steps.body: Medical procedures, including sterilisation, require the person's free and informed consent.

a.text: Arjun says he wants to spend time alone with his girlfriend. His parents…

choices.label: Talk with him about consent, relationships and safety in accessible ways
Forbid all relationships
Ignore safety completely

choices.label: Believe him, keep him safe and report it
Say he misunderstood

lessons.title: Where body worry comes from

scenes.text: Pallavi, 27, won't post photos without filters and avoids weddings.
Relatives comment on her 'dark skin' and weight.
A counsellor helps her notice where these messages come from.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor, pharmacist or qualified counsellor. In an emergency call **112**. Mental health support: **Tele-MANAS 14416** (free, 24×7).

steps.title: Sources
steps.body: Social media filters, advertising (fairness creams, weight-loss products), family comments, matrimonial pressure, gym culture, and pornography's unrealistic bodies.

steps.title: Colourism
steps.body: Skin colour has no link to health, beauty or worth. Fairness-product advertising has faced regulatory scrutiny in India; some brands dropped 'fair' from names in 2020.

steps.title: Weight stigma
steps.body: Shaming doesn't improve health; it's linked to avoiding doctors and disordered eating. Health is about habits, not just weight.

statements.s: Filters show what people really look like.
Skin colour relates to health or worth.
Weight shaming helps people get healthier.
Advertising profits from body insecurity.

options: Who profits from me feeling bad?

sources: Navtej Singh Johar v Union of India 2018

lessons.title: Genital-size and appearance anxiety

scenes.text: Imran, 25, worries his penis is 'too small' after watching porn.
He considers 'enlargement' pills online.
A urologist reassures him.

steps.title: Normal variation
steps.body: Genital size and appearance vary widely in all sexes. Most men who worry about penis size are within the normal range. Labia vary greatly in size, colour and symmetry — that's normal.

steps.title: Scams and risks
steps.body: 'Enlargement' pills, oils and devices are not proven and can be harmful. Cosmetic genital surgeries carry risks; seek reputable specialists and consider counselling first.

steps.title: Function over form
steps.body: Satisfaction in sex is linked far more to communication, comfort and connection than to size or appearance.

items.q: Is my penis too small?
items.a: Almost certainly within normal range. A urologist can reassure you privately.

items.q: Are my labia abnormal?
items.a: Labia naturally vary in size, colour and symmetry. Pain, itching or sores are reasons to see a doctor; appearance alone usually isn't.

items.q: Do enlargement pills work?
items.a: No reliable evidence — and some contain harmful substances.

items.q: Does size matter to partners?
items.a: Surveys suggest most partners care far more about connection and care.

quiz.q: Most men worried about size are…

sources: Navtej Singh Johar v Union of India 2018

lessons.title: Body dysmorphic disorder and self-compassion

scenes.text: Rohit spends 3 hours a day checking his hairline and has had two procedures.
He still feels 'hideous'.

steps.title: BDD
steps.body: Body dysmorphic disorder: preoccupation with perceived flaws that others barely notice, with repetitive behaviours (mirror checking, grooming, comparing, reassurance-seeking) and significant distress. Cosmetic procedures usually don't relieve it. Treatment: CBT and SSRIs.

steps.title: Self-compassion tools
steps.body: Speak to yourself like a friend; list what your body does for you; curate your feed; limit mirror checking; practise body neutrality ('my body lets me…').

steps.title: When to get help
steps.body: If body worries take over an hour a day, stop you going out or lead to repeated procedures — see a doctor.

activity.prompt: Write three things your body did for you this week that have nothing to do with how it looks.
activity.hint: E.g., carried groceries, hugged a friend, healed a cut.

quiz.q: When body worry takes over an hour a day…

lessons.title: Bisexuality and the 'phase' myth

scenes.text: Kriti, 28, has dated men and is now attracted to a woman.
Friends say she's 'confused' or 'it's a phase'.
She learns about bisexuality.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor, pharmacist or qualified counsellor. In an emergency call **112**. Mental health support: **Tele-MANAS 14416** (free, 24×7).

steps.title: What it means
steps.body: Bisexual people are attracted to more than one gender. Attraction may not be equal or constant over time. It's a valid orientation, not indecision.

steps.title: Health and stigma
steps.body: Bisexual people often face stigma from both straight and gay communities ('bi-erasure') and report high rates of anxiety and depression — linked to stigma, not orientation.

steps.title: Respect
steps.body: Don't demand someone 'pick a side'. A bisexual person in a relationship with one partner is still bisexual.

statements.s: Bisexuality is just a phase.
A bisexual person married to a man is still bisexual.
statements.why: Orientation isn't defined by current partner.

statements.s: Bi-erasure means ignoring or denying bisexuality.
Attraction must be equal to all genders.

options: Attraction to more than one gender

quiz.q: High anxiety among bi people is linked to…

sources: Navtej Singh Johar v Union of India 2018

lessons.title: Asexuality and aromanticism

scenes.text: Varun, 31, has never felt sexual attraction and feels broken.
He discovers the term asexual.
He feels relief and community.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: **Asexual (ace)**: little or no sexual attraction. **Aromantic (aro)**: little or no romantic attraction. It's a spectrum — e.g. demisexual people feel attraction only after a strong emotional bond.

steps.title: Not a disorder
steps.body: Asexuality is an orientation, not low libido from illness. A doctor may check for medical causes if there's a *change* in desire that causes distress, but lifelong asexuality is not a disease.

steps.title: Relationships
steps.body: Many asexual people have loving relationships, some including sex by mutual agreement, some not. Honest communication about needs matters.

items.q: Can asexual people be in relationships?
items.a: Yes — many are, romantic or otherwise.

items.q: Is asexuality a hormone problem?
items.a: No. It's an orientation. Medical checks are for distressing *changes* in desire.

items.q: What is demisexual?
items.a: Feeling sexual attraction only after a strong emotional bond.

items.q: Can asexual people marry?
items.a: Yes. Clear, honest communication with a partner about expectations is important.

sources: Navtej Singh Johar v Union of India 2018

lessons.title: Questioning later, mixed-orientation marriages and marriage pressure

scenes.text: Sunil, 40, married with children, realises he is gay.
He fears for his family.
He sees an affirming counsellor.

steps.title: Questioning later is common
steps.body: Many people understand their orientation or identity later in life, often because of past stigma. It doesn't make earlier love fake.

steps.title: Mixed-orientation marriages
steps.body: Couples navigate this differently — some separate, some stay together with new agreements. Honesty, counselling, children's wellbeing, and both partners' needs matter. The spouse's feelings (shock, grief, anger) are valid too.

steps.title: Marriage pressure
steps.body: Being forced into marriage harms both partners. Adults have the legal right to choose whether and whom to marry (as permitted by law). If pressured with threats, seek help (112; women's helpline 181).

scenes.text: Arvind, 32, has felt flat for three months, sleeps badly and has stopped playing cricket.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor, pharmacist or qualified counsellor. In an emergency call **112**. Mental health support: **Tele-MANAS 14416** (free, 24×7).

steps.title: What depression is
steps.body: A medical condition with persistent low mood and/or loss of interest for at least 2 weeks, plus changes in sleep, appetite, energy, concentration, self-worth, and sometimes thoughts of death. It affects functioning.

steps.title: How common
steps.body: WHO estimates depression affects hundreds of millions of people worldwide; it's a leading cause of disability. It is not weakness or a character flaw.

steps.title: Causes
steps.body: A mix of genes, stress, trauma, physical illness (thyroid, chronic pain), substances, sleep loss and life events — often no single cause.

steps.title: Treatment
steps.body: Psychotherapy (CBT, behavioural activation, interpersonal therapy), antidepressants for moderate–severe depression, exercise, sleep, social contact. Antidepressants usually take 2–6 weeks to help and should not be stopped suddenly.

statements.s: Depression is a character weakness.
Symptoms lasting 2+ weeks are part of the definition.
Antidepressants work overnight.
Exercise can help depression.

options: Low mood or loss of interest

lessons.title: Anxiety disorders: GAD, panic, social anxiety, phobias

scenes.text: Sanya, 26, suddenly feels her heart race, can't breathe and is sure she's dying in the metro.
The ECG is normal.
A psychiatrist explains panic disorder.

steps.title: Types
steps.body:
- **Generalised anxiety disorder**: constant hard-to-control worry about many things.
- **Panic disorder**: repeated unexpected panic attacks and fear of more.
- **Social anxiety disorder**: intense fear of judgment in social situations.
- **Specific phobias**: intense fear of particular things.

steps.title: Panic attacks peak and pass
steps.body: Panic symptoms usually peak within about 10 minutes. They feel terrifying but are not dangerous by themselves. First episodes of chest pain should still be medically checked.

steps.title: Treatment
steps.body: CBT (including exposure) is first-line; some medicines (such as SSRIs) help. Avoid relying on alcohol or sleeping pills — they worsen anxiety over time.

steps.title: In the moment
steps.body: Slow breathing (longer out-breath), naming 5 things you can see, and reminding yourself 'this will pass' help ride a wave.

steps.title: Your rights
steps.body: The Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 gives people the right to access mental-health care, confidentiality and dignity, and lets you make an 'advance directive' about future treatment.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor, pharmacist or qualified counsellor. In an emergency call **112**. Mental health support: **Tele-MANAS 14416** (free, 24×7).

steps.title: Obsessions and compulsions
steps.body: **Obsessions**: unwanted, intrusive thoughts, images or urges that cause anxiety (e.g. contamination, harm, doubt, taboo thoughts). **Compulsions**: repeated actions or mental rituals done to reduce the anxiety (checking, washing, counting, seeking reassurance).

steps.title: Intrusive thoughts don't mean you want them
steps.body: People with OCD are often distressed precisely because the thoughts go against their values. Having a thought is not the same as wanting or doing it.

steps.title: Treatment
steps.body: **Exposure and response prevention (ERP)** — a form of CBT — gradually faces the fear without performing the compulsion. SSRIs are also effective, often at higher doses, under a psychiatrist.

steps.title: Reassurance trap
steps.body: Family repeatedly reassuring ('Yes, the door is locked') can keep OCD going. Therapists help families respond supportively instead.

statements.s: OCD is just liking things tidy.
Intrusive thoughts mean the person secretly wants them.
ERP is an evidence-based treatment.
Constant reassurance helps OCD in the long run.

options: An action done to reduce obsession-related anxiety

lessons.title: Bipolar disorder: highs, lows and the in-between

scenes.text: Rohan, 24, hasn't slept for four nights, talks fast, and spent his savings on a 'genius' business.
His sister is scared.

steps.title: What it is
steps.body: Bipolar disorder involves episodes of **mania** or **hypomania** and usually **depression**, with periods of stable mood in between. It's different from normal mood swings.

steps.title: Types
steps.body:
- **Bipolar I**: at least one manic episode (severe; may need hospital; can include psychosis).
- **Bipolar II**: hypomania (milder highs) plus major depressive episodes.

steps.title: Treatment
steps.body: Mood stabilisers (such as lithium, with regular blood tests), some antipsychotics, psychotherapy and routine. Antidepressants alone can trigger mania in some people — a psychiatrist balances this.

steps.title: Warning signs to watch
steps.body: Reduced need for sleep, racing thoughts, unusual spending, irritability — and on the low side, withdrawal. A relapse plan agreed while well helps.

items.text: Little need for sleep but full of energy

scenes.text: When stable, Rohan writes a relapse plan with his psychiatrist and sister.

steps.title: Stability habits
steps.body: Regular sleep and routine, taking medicines as prescribed, limiting alcohol and avoiding drugs, tracking mood, and early contact with the care team.

steps.title: For family
steps.body: Learn the illness, notice early signs, avoid blame, agree in advance what you'll do if signs appear (with consent). Look after your own wellbeing too.

steps.title: Rights at work
steps.body: The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 includes mental illness as a disability category, and supports reasonable accommodation.

scenes.text: Vivek, 21, starts hearing voices commenting on him and believes neighbours are spying.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor, pharmacist or qualified counsellor. In an emergency call **112**. Mental health support: **Tele-MANAS 14416** (free, 24×7).

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: **Psychosis** is losing touch with reality, including **hallucinations** (hearing, seeing or feeling things others don't) and **delusions** (fixed false beliefs, like being followed or controlled). Thinking and speech can become disorganised.

steps.title: Causes
steps.body: Psychosis can occur in schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, severe depression, postpartum, with drugs (cannabis — especially high-potency and early use — stimulants, alcohol withdrawal), and medical conditions (infections, brain disorders). It needs medical assessment.

steps.title: Not black magic, not weakness
steps.body: It is a treatable health condition. Delaying care for rituals or faith healers can worsen outcomes; faith and medical care can go together.

statements.s: Hallucinations are perceptions without an external source.
Psychosis is caused by black magic.
Cannabis can trigger psychosis in some people.
Psychosis always means schizophrenia.

scenes.text: Vivek starts an antipsychotic and family sessions.
He returns to college part-time a year later.
He still has check-ups but is doing well.

steps.title: How common
steps.body: WHO estimates schizophrenia affects about 1 in 300 people worldwide. It usually begins in late teens to early 30s.

steps.title: Symptom groups
steps.body: **Positive**: hallucinations, delusions. **Negative**: reduced motivation, emotion and speech. **Cognitive**: attention and memory problems. Diagnosis requires symptoms lasting a significant period and excludes other causes.

steps.title: Treatment
steps.body: Antipsychotic medicines (tablets or long-acting injections), psychoeducation, family therapy, CBT for psychosis, rehabilitation and supported employment. Early intervention improves outcomes.

steps.title: Myths
steps.body: Schizophrenia is not 'split personality'. Most people with schizophrenia are not violent and are more likely to be victims of violence than perpetrators.

quiz.q: People with schizophrenia are more likely to be…

steps.title: Do
steps.body: Stay calm, speak simply, give space, don't argue with the delusion but acknowledge feelings ('That sounds frightening'), remove dangers, and contact their doctor, Tele-MANAS 14416, or 112 if there's risk.

steps.title: Don't
steps.body: Don't mock, threaten, restrain unless absolutely necessary for safety, or try to 'prove' them wrong in the moment.

steps.title: The law
steps.body: Under the Mental Healthcare Act 2017, people have rights to dignity, and admission procedures (including supported admission) have safeguards. Chaining or inhumane treatment is prohibited.

scenes.text: Karthik, 33, is brilliant but always late, loses keys daily and misses deadlines.

A psychiatrist diagnoses ADHD.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor, pharmacist or qualified counsellor. In an emergency call **112**. Mental health support: **Tele-MANAS 14416** (free, 24×7).

steps.title: What it is
steps.body: A neurodevelopmental condition starting in childhood, with inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity that causes problems in more than one setting. Many adults were never diagnosed as children, especially women.

steps.title: Adult signs
steps.body: Disorganisation, time-blindness, procrastination, restlessness, impulsive decisions, emotional reactivity, hyperfocus on interesting tasks, difficulty finishing boring tasks.

steps.title: Treatment
steps.body: Medicines (stimulant and non-stimulant, prescribed and monitored by a psychiatrist), coaching, CBT for ADHD, and environment changes. Treat coexisting anxiety, depression or substance use.

steps.title: Practical strategies
steps.body: External reminders, timers, body-doubling, breaking tasks down, visible to-do lists, routines for keys/wallet.

statements.s: ADHD only affects children.
Adults with ADHD are lazy.
Hyperfocus can occur in ADHD.
Medication must be prescribed and monitored.

quiz.q: A common adult ADHD sign is…

scenes.text: Tanya, 22, has lost a lot of weight, skips meals, and exercises for hours.
She faints at the gym.
Doctors diagnose anorexia nervosa.

steps.title: Main types
steps.body:
- **Anorexia nervosa**: restriction, low weight, intense fear of weight gain.
- **Bulimia nervosa**: binge eating followed by compensating (vomiting, laxatives, fasting, over-exercise).
- **Binge-eating disorder**: recurrent binges with distress, without regular compensation.
- Also ARFID (avoidant/restrictive intake).

steps.title: Serious illnesses
steps.body: Eating disorders have among the highest death rates of mental illnesses, from medical complications and suicide. They affect all genders, ages, body sizes and backgrounds — you can't tell by looking.

steps.title: Medical red flags
steps.body: Fainting, chest pain, very slow pulse, vomiting blood, confusion — emergency care (112).

steps.title: Treatment
steps.body: Specialist team: medical monitoring, nutrition rehabilitation, therapy (CBT-E; family-based treatment for younger people), treatment of coexisting conditions.

scenes.text: Sameer, 35, posts 'Nothing matters anymore' and gives away his guitar.
His friend Joseph notices.
Joseph reaches out.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor, pharmacist or qualified counsellor. In an emergency call **112**. Mental health support: **Tele-MANAS 14416** (free, 24×7).

steps.title: Suicide is preventable
steps.body: Many people who feel suicidal are ambivalent and respond to support. Help works.

steps.title: Warning signs
steps.body: Talking about wanting to die or being a burden, hopelessness, withdrawing, giving things away, saying goodbye, sudden calm after depression, increased alcohol/drug use, searching for ways to die.

steps.title: Self-harm
steps.body: Self-harm is often a way to cope with overwhelming emotion. It needs compassionate care, not punishment. Treat wounds medically and seek mental-health support.

steps.title: Law
steps.body: Under the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017, a person who attempts suicide is presumed to be under severe stress and should receive care, not punishment.

steps.title: Myths
steps.body: Asking about suicide does NOT plant the idea. People who talk about it can be at risk. Most suicidal crises are temporary.

statements.s: Asking someone about suicide puts the idea in their head.
statements.why: Research shows asking can reduce distress.

statements.s: Giving away belongings can be a warning sign.
Suicide is preventable.
Self-harm should be punished.

quiz.q: The MHCA 2017 treats attempted suicide as…
options: A sign of severe stress needing care

quiz.q: Sudden calm after severe depression may…

scenes.text: Joseph calls Sameer: 'Your post worried me.'
He asks: 'Are you thinking about killing yourself?'
Sameer says yes — and talks for an hour.

steps.title: Ask directly
steps.body: 'Are you thinking about suicide?' A clear question shows you can handle the answer.

steps.title: Listen
steps.body: Don't rush to fix or lecture. Reflect: 'It sounds like you've been carrying so much.' Avoid 'you have so much to live for' — it can feel dismissive.

steps.title: Stay and connect
steps.body: Don't leave someone at immediate risk alone. Call Tele-MANAS 14416 together, or 112 if in immediate danger. Help them reach a doctor.

steps.title: Safe messaging
steps.body: When talking or posting about suicide, don't describe methods or locations, avoid sensational words, and always include help resources.

choices.label: 'Are you thinking about suicide?'
'Don't say silly things.'

choices.feedback: Never leave someone at risk alone.

steps.title: A safety plan
steps.body: 1) My warning signs. 2) Things I can do to cope. 3) People and places that distract me. 4) People I can ask for help. 5) Professionals and helplines (14416, 112). 6) Making my environment safer.

steps.title: Means safety
steps.body: Putting time and distance between a person in crisis and dangerous means (e.g. a trusted person holding medicines, locking away pesticides) saves lives, because crises often pass.

steps.title: Follow up
steps.body: The period after a crisis or hospital discharge carries raised risk — regular check-ins matter.

lessons.title: Forms of abuse and coercive control

scenes.text: At first Rakesh 'just wanted to know' where Divya was.
Soon he checked her phone, controlled her salary and cut her off from friends.
He never hit her, so she thought it wasn't abuse.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor, pharmacist or qualified counsellor. In an emergency call **112**. Mental health support: **Tele-MANAS 14416** (free, 24×7).

steps.title: Forms
steps.body:
- **Physical**: hitting, pushing, restraining.
- **Emotional/verbal**: insults, threats, humiliation, gaslighting.
- **Sexual**: any forced or coerced sexual act.
- **Economic**: controlling money, stopping work, taking salary, dowry demands.
- **Digital**: tracking, demanding passwords, sharing private images.

steps.title: Coercive control
steps.body: A pattern of controlling, isolating, monitoring and intimidating behaviour that strips someone's freedom — sometimes without physical violence. It's abuse.

steps.title: Anyone can be affected
steps.body: Abuse happens across class, caste, religion, gender and orientation. Men and LGBTQ+ people can also experience abuse.

steps.title: Escalation signs
steps.body: Threats to kill, strangulation (choking), weapons, threats around separation, and pregnancy-related violence raise the risk of serious harm — seek help urgently.

items.text: Partner asks how your day was
Partner takes your salary every month

options: A pattern of control and isolation

sources: Joseph Shine v Union of India 2018

lessons.title: Safety planning

scenes.text: Divya quietly prepares documents and a phone with numbers.
She saves 112 and 181.
She identifies a friend's house to go to.

steps.title: A safety plan
steps.body: Know safe rooms (avoid kitchens/bathrooms with no exit), keep a charged phone, memorise key numbers, agree a code word with a trusted person, keep copies of documents (ID, bank, certificates) and some money somewhere safe.

steps.title: Leaving can be the riskiest time
steps.body: Plan carefully and get support from a helpline, protection officer or NGO when preparing to leave.

steps.title: Digital safety
steps.body: Check for location sharing, unknown apps, and shared accounts; use a safe device to seek help; clear browsing history if safe to do so.

items: Agree a code word with a trusted person
Keep copies of ID and bank documents in a safe place
Identify a place I can go quickly
Check my phone for tracking/location sharing

quiz.q: Which rooms are least safe in an argument?
The time of leaving can be…

lessons.title: The law in general terms

scenes.text: Divya meets a Protection Officer under the PWDVA.
She learns about protection and residence orders.

steps.title: PWDVA 2005
steps.body: The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act provides civil remedies: **protection orders**, **residence orders** (right to stay in the shared household), **monetary relief**, **custody orders** and **compensation**. Complaints can be made through a Protection Officer, police, or directly to a magistrate.

steps.title: Criminal law (BNS, in force from 1 July 2024)
steps.body: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita criminalises cruelty by a husband or his relatives (the provision that replaced IPC 498A), dowry death, assault, and criminal intimidation. Dowry demands are also offences under the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961.

steps.title: Free legal aid
steps.body: Women are entitled to free legal aid through Legal Services Authorities. NGOs and One Stop Centres ('Sakhi') offer shelter, medical, police and legal help. This is general education, not legal advice.

statements.s: The PWDVA can grant a woman the right to stay in the shared household.

courses.title: Separation & divorce in India: facts in general terms
courses.summary: How divorce works in general terms under different personal laws, mutual-consent divorce, maintenance, child custody principles, and emotional coping — without stigma.
outcomes: Describe mutual-consent and contested divorce in general terms

lessons.title: How divorce works — general terms

scenes.text: Neha and Siddharth have lived separately for over a year and both want a divorce.
A family lawyer explains mutual consent.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor, pharmacist or qualified counsellor. In an emergency call **112**. Mental health support: **Tele-MANAS 14416** (free, 24×7).

steps.title: Personal laws
steps.body: Divorce rules depend on the law governing the marriage: Hindu Marriage Act 1955 (Hindus, Sikhs, Jains, Buddhists), Special Marriage Act 1954 (civil/inter-faith), Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act 1939 and Muslim personal law, Indian Divorce Act 1869 (Christians), Parsi Marriage and Divorce Act 1936.

steps.title: Mutual consent (e.g. HMA Section 13B)
steps.body: Spouses who have lived separately for at least a year and agree to divorce file a joint petition; there is a waiting period of six months before the second motion, which the Supreme Court has held can be waived in suitable cases.

steps.title: Contested divorce
steps.body: One spouse seeks divorce on legal grounds, such as cruelty, desertion, adultery, or others listed in the relevant law. It usually takes longer.

steps.title: Instant triple talaq
steps.body: Pronouncing instant triple talaq is void and a criminal offence under the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019. This is general education, not legal advice.

statements.s: All Indians follow the same divorce law.
statements.why: Depends on personal law/Special Marriage Act.

statements.s: Mutual-consent divorce under HMA needs at least one year of separation.
The six-month waiting period can sometimes be waived.
Instant triple talaq is valid.

quiz.q: Mutual-consent divorce under the HMA is Section…
Inter-faith civil marriages are governed by…

sources: Joseph Shine v Union of India 2018

lessons.title: Maintenance, property and custody principles

scenes.text: Neha worries about money and their 6-year-old daughter.
Her lawyer explains maintenance and custody.

steps.title: Maintenance
steps.body: A spouse unable to maintain themselves, children and dependent parents can seek maintenance — under personal laws, the PWDVA, and BNSS Section 144 (which replaced CrPC Section 125). Courts consider income, needs and standard of living.

steps.title: Stridhan
steps.body: A woman's stridhan (gifts received before, at or after marriage) is her property and must be returned.

steps.title: Custody
steps.body: Courts decide by the **welfare of the child** — the paramount consideration. Options include custody to one parent with visitation, or shared parenting arrangements. Children's wishes may be considered as they grow older.

steps.title: Documents
steps.body: Keep records: income, expenses, assets, children's needs, and any abuse evidence. This is general education, not legal advice.

activity.prompt: Questions people are embarrassed to ask

items.q: Will I lose my children if I'm the one who leaves?
items.a: Courts decide on the child's welfare, not on who left. Talk to a lawyer about your situation.

items.q: Can men get maintenance?
items.a: Under some laws (e.g. HMA sections), either spouse can seek maintenance depending on circumstances.

items.q: Is stridhan mine after divorce?
items.a: Yes, stridhan is the woman's property.

items.q: Can I get free legal help?
items.a: Women, children and people with low income are eligible for free legal aid via Legal Services Authorities.

sources: Joseph Shine v Union of India 2018

lessons.title: Emotional coping and helping children

scenes.text: Siddharth feels relief and grief at the same time.
Their daughter asks 'Is it my fault?'
They agree on a co-parenting plan.

steps.title: Mixed feelings are normal
steps.body: Grief, relief, anger, guilt and fear can coexist. Divorce stigma can add shame — divorce is a legal decision, not a moral failure.

steps.title: Telling children
steps.body: Tell them together if possible, in age-appropriate words: 'This is a grown-up decision. It's not your fault. We both love you.' Keep routines; don't make children messengers or criticise the other parent in front of them.

steps.title: Seek support
steps.body: Counselling, support groups, Tele-MANAS 14416. Watch for prolonged low mood in yourself or your children.

activity.hint: Include: not your fault, both love you, what stays the same.

lessons.title: Why affairs happen — and what they aren't

scenes.text: Priya discovers months of intimate messages between her husband Vinod and a colleague.
She feels shock, rage and humiliation.
A counsellor helps her make sense of it.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor, pharmacist or qualified counsellor. In an emergency call **112**. Mental health support: **Tele-MANAS 14416** (free, 24×7).

steps.title: Many forms
steps.body: Physical affairs, emotional affairs (intense secret emotional intimacy), online relationships, and secret use of dating apps. What counts as betrayal depends on the couple's agreements.

steps.title: Contributors
steps.body: Unmet needs, distance, opportunity, unresolved personal issues, low self-worth, thrill-seeking, alcohol. These *explain* — they don't excuse. The person who cheated is responsible for their choice.

steps.title: Not always the end
steps.body: Many couples separate after infidelity; others rebuild, often with counselling. Both are valid outcomes.

statements.s: Emotional affairs can be as painful as physical ones.
statements.why: Betrayal is about secrecy and intimacy.

statements.s: Explaining an affair excuses it.
Every couple separates after infidelity.
The betrayed partner caused the affair.
statements.why: The choice belongs to the person who cheated.

options: Secret intense emotional intimacy outside the relationship

sources: Joseph Shine v Union of India 2018

lessons.title: After discovery: health, emotions and the law

scenes.text: Priya can't sleep or eat.
Her friend suggests STI testing.
She asks whether adultery is a crime.

steps.title: Immediate steps
steps.body: Look after basics — sleep, food, support from one or two trusted people. Avoid big decisions or public posts in the first days. If physical intimacy occurred outside the relationship, both partners should consider STI testing.

steps.title: Law in general terms
steps.body: In 2018 the Supreme Court (Joseph Shine v Union of India) struck down adultery as a criminal offence. Adultery remains a ground for divorce under personal laws. This is general education, not legal advice.

steps.title: Safety
steps.body: If discovery leads to threats or violence, call 112. Infidelity never justifies abuse.

items.q: Is it normal to obsess over details?
items.a: Yes — intrusive thoughts are common after betrayal. A counsellor can help manage them.

items.q: Should I get tested?
items.a: If sexual contact happened outside the relationship, STI testing is sensible for both partners.

items.q: Can I file a criminal case for adultery?
items.a: Adultery is no longer a crime in India (2018), but it can be a ground for divorce.

items.q: Should I decide right away?
items.a: Usually it's wiser to wait until the initial shock settles, unless you're unsafe.

options: Not a crime; a divorce ground

lessons.title: Rebuilding trust — or parting well

scenes.text: Vinod ends the affair, answers questions honestly, and goes to therapy.
Trust grows slowly, with setbacks.
Priya decides to keep working on it.

steps.title: Stages often described
steps.body: 1) **Atonement**: full ending of the affair, honesty, remorse without defensiveness. 2) **Attunement**: understanding what happened and rebuilding emotional connection. 3) **Attachment**: renewed intimacy and new agreements.

steps.title: What helps
steps.body: Transparency agreed by both, consistency over time, patience with triggers, couples therapy. The hurt partner sets the pace.

steps.title: Parting well
steps.body: If you separate, aim for respect, protect children from conflict, and get legal and emotional support.

lessons.title: The money talk

scenes.text: Ananya and Rohit realise they've never discussed money.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice

steps.title: Talk about
steps.body: Incomes, debts (loans, credit cards), savings, support for parents/siblings, goals (home, children, travel), spending styles, and who manages what.

steps.title: Money date
steps.body: Monthly, calm, with tea and numbers. Use 'I' statements and focus on shared goals.

steps.body: Supporting parents is common in India; agree openly on how much and how, so neither partner feels ignored.

lessons.title: Joint, separate or both?

scenes.text: Ananya and Rohit choose 'yours, mine, ours'.
Each contributes proportionally to income.

steps.title: Systems
steps.body: **Fully joint**, **fully separate**, or **hybrid** (joint for household, personal accounts for each). Proportional contributions can feel fairer when incomes differ.

steps.title: Unpaid work counts
steps.body: Caregiving and housework have economic value. A partner who leaves paid work for family should still have access to money and savings in their own name.

steps.title: Both should know
steps.body: Both partners should know where accounts, policies and investments are and how to access them.

a.text: Rohit earns twice what Ananya does. Fair household split?

choices.label: Proportional contributions based on income

choices.label: Agree she keeps personal savings and access to joint funds
Close her account

end.text: They write their plan down and review it each year.

lessons.title: Financial abuse, dowry and protection

scenes.text: After the wedding, in-laws demand a car 'as promised'.
Shalini's husband takes her salary card.

steps.title: Dowry is illegal
steps.body: Giving, taking or demanding dowry is an offence under the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961. Dowry harassment and cruelty are offences under the BNS. Call 181 or 112 if threatened.

steps.title: Financial abuse
steps.body: Taking someone's salary or cards, stopping them working, running up debts in their name, or forcing them to sign documents is economic abuse under the PWDVA.

steps.title: Protect each other
steps.body: Nominations on every account and policy, adequate term life and health insurance, a written will, and both names known to family. Keep important documents accessible to both. This is general education, not financial or legal advice.

Taking a partner's salary card without consent can be economic abuse.

lessons.title: Boundaries with respect

scenes.text: Sunita's mother-in-law enters their room without knocking and comments on her cooking daily.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor, pharmacist or qualified counsellor. In an emergency call **112**. Mental health support: **Tele-MANAS 14416** (free, 24×7).

steps.title: What boundaries are
steps.body: Boundaries are what *you* will do to protect your wellbeing, stated calmly — not attempts to control others.

steps.title: Scripts
steps.body:
- 'Please knock before coming in — we value a little privacy.'
- 'I know you love cooking this way; I'll try my way tonight.'
- 'We'll decide that together and let you know.'

steps.title: Respect both ways
steps.body: Elders may come from different expectations. Appreciation plus clear limits works better than silent resentment or explosive fights.

lessons.title: The spouse in the middle

scenes.text: Amit feels caught between his mother and his wife.
A counsellor coaches him to become a bridge, not a messenger.

steps.title: United front
steps.body: Couples decide together in private, then each speaks to their own family. 'We've decided' prevents playing one against the other.

steps.title: Each handles their own family
steps.body: Usually, each spouse addresses issues with their own parents — it's received better.

steps.title: Silence isn't neutral
steps.body: A spouse who never intervenes leaves their partner alone. Support doesn't mean disrespecting parents.

steps.title: Your decisions
steps.body: Whether and when to have children, careers, and lifestyle are the couple's decisions. Reproductive choices belong especially to the person who would be pregnant.

steps.title: Deflecting lines
steps.body: 'We'll share news when there is any!' 'We've thought about it and this works for us.' Infertility may be private pain — others' questions can hurt.

steps.title: When pressure becomes abuse
steps.body: Threats, confinement, taking documents or salary, forcing someone to quit work, or harassment for dowry or a male child are abuse. Sex selection is illegal (PCPNDT Act). Call 181 or 112.
